en: The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra*, Volume One.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Eastern Jin Records.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the community of bhikṣus...

There were more than ten thousand people—including bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, kings, ministers, elders, commoners, and those who followed the ninety-six kinds of paths—who daily listened to the sūtras before the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"The assembly of people grows larger by the day, and my body finds no peace.
The Buddha desired to leave the assembly and go to a secluded place to sit in meditation and contemplate the Way.
The Buddha then left the assembly and entered the mountains, arriving among the Khadira grove; there was a deity dwelling in those trees.
The Buddha sat beneath them and contemplated the path of purity.

Not far from the grove of trees, there was a herd of more than five hundred elephants; among them was an elephant king, noble and virtuous, who understood matters of good and evil just as a human being does.
The herd of elephants was numerous, surrounding the elephant king on all sides; among them were males and females, those with long tusks, medium tusks, and short tusks.

When the elephant king became thirsty and wished to go drink water, the young elephants ran ahead into the water to drink; having drunk, they ran and played about in the water, churning and stirring it until it became turbid and foul, so that the elephant king could not obtain clear water to drink.

When the elephant king, being hungry, wished to go out to eat grass, the young elephants ran ahead of him to graze upon the choice grass; as they ran and frolicked, they trampled it down, so that the elephant king was unable to obtain pure grass to eat.
The Elephant King thought to himself:

"My herd suffers from many afflictions; these elephants and young elephant calves stir up the water until it is turbid and make the grass unclean, yet they return to their habit of drinking that turbid water and eating the grass trampled underfoot."
The elephant king thought to himself, "I wish to abandon these elephants and go to a secluded place; how pleasant that would be!
The elephant king then left the herd and proceeded into the mountains, entering among the *kadalī* groves.

When the Elephant King saw the Buddha sitting beneath a tree, his heart was filled with great joy; he then approached the Buddha, bowed his head and knelt to pay homage to him, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I have left the multitude and come to this place; the elephant king has likewise left his herd and come to these trees. Their circumstances are exactly the same."
The Buddha preached this sutra for the Elephant King, saying:
"The Buddha is the most honored among humans; the Elephant King is likewise the most honored among elephants.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"My mind and the mind of the Elephant King are perfectly attuned; I and the Elephant King shall both delight together in this grove.

When the Elephant King had finished listening to the sutra, his mind was immediately opened and enlightened; understanding the Buddha’s intent, he looked toward the place where the Buddha was pacing back and forth, took water with his trunk and sprinkled it upon the ground, gathered grass with his trunk and swept the ground, and trod the earth with his feet to make it level and smooth.
The Elephant King attended upon him morning and evening every day.
After a long time had passed in this manner, the Buddha departed for the unconditioned realm of Nirvana.
Not knowing the Buddha’s whereabouts, the Elephant King wandered about in search of him; failing to find the Buddha, he wept in sorrow and distress, finding no joy and not daring to eat or drink.

At that time, there was a Buddhist monastery in the country situated on a mountain called Karavāna. Within it resided five hundred śramaṇas who had all attained the path of arhatship; they would regularly recite the sūtras until dawn on the six fast days of each month.
The elephant king was also on the mountain, near the monastery.
Knowing that there were days for the recitation of the scriptures during the six fast days, on those days the elephant king would regularly go into the monastery to listen to the teachings.

The śramaṇas knew that the elephant king delighted in listening to the sūtras; whenever they wished to recite the sūtras, they would wait for the elephant king to arrive before beginning their recitation.
The elephant king listened to the sūtras until dawn, neither sleeping nor lying down, remaining motionless and unshakable.
Because the Elephant King had frequently heard the sutras and served the Buddha, after a long time he too reached the end of his life and died, whereupon he was reborn as the son of a human being.

He was born into a Brahmin family; however, no longer hearing the Buddha's sutras nor seeing any śramaṇas, he left home to enter the deep mountains to study the path of the Brahmins, dwelling there upon the mountain.
Not far away, there was also a Brahmin practitioner who lived on the mountain together with him; they frequented one another and shared a close friendship.
One of them thought to himself:

"I am weary of the anxieties and sufferings of worldly officials, and of old age, sickness, and death. Hereafter, I shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, amidst poverty and destitution."
"For this reason, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and become a śramaṇa, seeking the path of world-transcending unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*).
Another man thought to himself:
"I wish to seek the status of a king and attain sovereign power, so that all the people of the world shall belong to me and follow my commands."
Thus did the two of them both make their vow.
After a long time, the two each reached the end of their lives and were reborn as humans in the world.
One of them, who in his previous existence had desired to become a king, was born on the seashore as the crown prince of a king; his parents named him Milinda.
One among them, who in his previous life had sought the path of liberation, the unconditioned Nirvana, was born in the district of Jibin in India; his parents named him Dharmaruci.
As soon as he was born, he was clad in the *kāṣāya* robes; that he was born together with the robes was due to his original vow in a former life.
In his family, there was also an elephant king born on the same day. In India, elephants are called *nāga*; thus, his parents named the child Nāgasena after the elephant.
When Nāgasena grew up, he was fifteen or sixteen years old and had an uncle named Lohan.

Lohan had become a *śramaṇa* and possessed peerless, extraordinary talent that was without equal in the world. His eyes could see through solid objects and his ears could hear through them; he knew the origins of his own past lives. When he walked, he could fly; he could emerge from solid matter without resistance and enter into it as if through no opening. He exercised mastery over transformations, performing anything at will. Regarding the thoughts in the minds of all beings, from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth down to the smallest crawling insects, Lohan knew them all in advance.
Nagasena then went in person to his maternal uncle, Kesi, and said to him:
"My intention is to follow the Way of the Buddha; I wish to shave my hair and beard, don the *kāṣāya*, and become a śramaṇa. Now, I shall become your disciple."
"Would you rather take me as a śramaṇa?
Knowing that Nāgasena had performed good deeds in his past lives and possessed wisdom, Lohan felt great compassion for him and consequently permitted him to become a śrāmaṇera.

Nāgasena had first become a novice śrāmaṇera and received the ten precepts; daily he recited the sūtras and pursued his studies, and through contemplating the sūtras and the precepts, he attained the four dhyānas and came to fully understand all the scriptures, yet alone he had not yet received the great śramaṇa ordination.
At that time, there was a Buddhist monastery on a mountain in the kingdom named Huṛcan; within Huṛcan Monastery there were five hundred śramaṇas, all of whom had attained the path of arhatship.
Among them was a foremost Arhat named Āṣāḍha, who was able to know the past, future, and present affairs of both the heavens and the human world.
When Nāgasena reached the age of twenty, he became a great śramaṇa and received the precepts of a great śramaṇa; he then went to the Veṇuvana Monastery and approached the place where Āṣāḍha was.

At that time, five hundred Arhats were seated in the lecture hall on the fifteenth day to recite the Mahāśramaṇa-Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the Great Śramaṇas had all entered, and Nāgasena was also among them.

When all the śramaṇas were seated, Aśvajit observed that the minds of all the śramaṇas in the assembly were those of arhats, with the sole exception of Nāgasena, who had not yet attained the path of an arhat.
Aṭṭhaka said, "The *Upamā-sūtra* states:
'If one enters a granary of husked rice, if there is black rice among the pure white grains, it is immediately picked out as being of poor quality.
Now, within my assembly all are pure and white; only Nātaputta is black, for he has not yet attained the path of an Arhat.'"
When Nāgasena heard Āṣāḍha reciting the sūtra in this manner, great anxiety arose within him; he paid homage to the five hundred śramaṇas and immediately departed.
Nāgasena thought to himself:
"It is not fitting for me to remain seated in this assembly; I have not yet attained liberation, whereas these other śramaṇas have all already attained it."
It is as if there were a fox or a dog among a pride of lions; I am now just like that.
From this day forward, if I do not attain the Way, I shall no longer sit among the assembly.
Aṭṭhaka, knowing Nāgasena’s intention, called him forward and stroked the top of his head with his hand, saying:
"You shall attain arhatship before long; do not be sorrowful."
Āṣāḍha said, "I wish to sit and stay with Nāgasena.
Nāgasena had another teacher, over eighty years of age, named Kātyāyana.
In that district there was an upāsaka who was very virtuous and good, who daily provided meals for Kātyāyana and his disciples.

When Nāgasena arrived, he acted as the teacher’s attendant and went to fetch the alms bowl; the teacher then instructed Nāgasena to go to the house of a lay devotee to fetch the meal while holding water in his mouth.

The lay follower saw that Nāgasena was young and handsome, with conduct far surpassing that of others; he had long known him to possess wisdom and had previously heard of his reputation for clear aspiration and his ability to expound the sutras and the Way.
When the upāsaka saw Nāgasena enter his house, he immediately rose, went forward to pay his respects, and with palms joined together, said:
"I have provided meals for various śramaṇas for a long time, yet never before has anyone preached the Sūtras to me."
"Now I first seek your compassion; I pray that you will preach the sutras for me and dispel my ignorance.
Nāgasena then thought to himself:
"I have received my teacher's instruction that I must not speak while water is held in my mouth."
"I have now spat out water because I violated my teacher's precepts;
what should I do about this? Nāgasena thought:
"This upāsaka is also a man of great talent and high resolve. If I preach the Sūtras to him, I believe he will immediately attain the Way."
Nāgasena then spat out the water and sat down; he then preached the Sūtra for him:

"If a person practices giving, performs good deeds, and observes the precepts, they will enjoy peace and security in this life and be reborn in the heavens in the next. If they are subsequently reborn among humans, they shall possess clear wisdom and wealth and honor, and thereafter shall never again enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."
"Those who do not practice the sutras and precepts will suffer in this present life and, in future lives, will again fall into the three evil realms from which there is no time of escape.
Upon hearing this sutra, the upāsaka’s heart was immediately filled with joy.
That elder-upāsaka, his heart filled with joy, then spoke again of the profound sutra, saying:
"All things in the world must pass away; nothing remains forever."
All things that have passed away are suffering; the human body in this world is likewise.
People of the world all say:
"This is my body; it belongs to me."
All these have not yet attained the path of nirvāṇa with mastery.

As for those who possess the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa, they are neither born, nor do they age, nor are they ill, nor do they die; they are without grief and without anxiety, and all evils and arduous sufferings are entirely extinguished.
After Nāgasena had finished preaching the sutra, the lay follower immediately attained the first fruit of the path, the stage of Srotāpanna; Nāgasena himself also attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The lay follower was greatly rejoiced and prepared a fine, delicious meal for Nāgasena.
Nāgasena said to the lay follower,
"First take some food and place it in your teacher's bowl.
When Nāgasena had finished eating and completed his ritual rinsing of the mouth, he took the eating utensils and returned them to his teacher.
When the Master saw the meal utensils, he said:
"If you had brought these meal utensils today, it would have been excellent.
You have already offended the assembly; according to our agreement, you shall be expelled."
Nāgasena was distressed and unhappy.
His teacher said:
"Gather the assembly of bhikṣus."
When the community of bhikṣus had all assembled and taken their seats, the teacher said:
"Nāgasena has violated the agreement of us all; we shall expel him together, so that he may no longer remain among the assembly."
Āṣāḍha spoke by way of a simile:
"It is like a man who, holding a single arrow, shoots at two targets; such a person as this should not be driven out.
Nāgasena has himself attained the Way and has also caused the upāsaka to attain the Way; he should not be driven out."
The teacher Nāgasena said:
"Even if one were to hit a hundred targets with a single arrow, one would still be bound by the agreement of the multitude and could not remain there.
No other person can attain the Way as Nāgasena has; he shall indeed cut off the past and leave no successor."
When they did not expel Nāgasena, the others followed suit, making it impossible to turn them back later.
Those present in the assembly all remained silent and, following the teacher’s instruction, immediately expelled Nāgasena.

Nāgasena then placed his head at the feet of his teacher, rose, and performed prostrations to the entire community of bhikṣus. Having finished his salutations, he departed, entered deep into the mountains, and sat beneath a tree. Day and night he practiced with diligence, contemplating the Way without slackening. Thereupon, he spontaneously attained the path of an Arhat; he was able to fly, possessed the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience, could know the thoughts in the minds of others, and knew of himself the origins from which he had come in previous lives.

Having attained arhatship, he immediately returned to the Vairaṇyā Monastery. Among the assembly of bhikṣus, he prostrated himself, seeking pity and repenting for his transgressions before the bhikṣu-saṃgha of Vairaṇyā. The bhikṣu-saṃgha granted him their pardon; having completed his salutations, Nāgasena departed.

Nāgasena then traveled through various commanderies, counties, streets, lanes, and alleys, preaching the sūtras and precepts for the people and instructing them in goodness. Among them, some received the five precepts; some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; some attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; some attained the stage of *anāgāmin*; and some became śramaṇas and attained the stage of *arhat*. The first, the Four Heavenly Kings; the second, Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; and the seventh, Brahmā Devānām-Indra, all came before Nāgasena and paid him homage, bowing their heads to his feet and then withdrawing to sit. Nāgasena preached the sūtras for all these people, and his fame spread throughout the four worlds.
Wherever Nāgasena traveled, all the devas, humans, spirits, and nāgas who saw him were without exception filled with joy, and they all obtained merit.
Nāgasena then traveled to the kingdom of Śākala in India and stayed at the Khemaka Monastery.
There was a former acquaintance from his previous life who was the crown prince of a king by the seaside; his name was Milinda.

From his youth, Milinda delighted in reading the scriptures and studying heterodox paths; he thoroughly mastered the doctrines and texts of these heterodox schools, such that no heterodox practitioner could defeat him in debate.
When his father, the king, passed away, Milinda was immediately established as the monarch.
The king asked his ministers at his side, saying,
"Among the practitioners and the people within the kingdom, who is able to debate the difficult points of the Way with me?
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
“There are. Those who study the Buddha-way are called śramaṇas by people; they possess broad and penetrating wisdom and are able to engage in debate on the profound path with Your Majesty.”

He is currently in the Great Qin Kingdom in the north; the kingdom is named Shajie, and it is the palace of an ancient king. Within and without the country all is peaceful and secure, and the people are entirely virtuous.
The city is square, with double roads running along its perimeter, and all the city gates are adorned with intricate carvings and engravings.

The women of the palace each had their respective quarters; the various streets and market towns were arranged in orderly rows; the main thoroughfares were broad with shops lined up in succession; and there was a great multitude of men and women on elephants, horses, chariots, and foot, including gatekeepers, mendicants, kinsmen, artisans, and commoners.

Furthermore, the various small kingdoms are mostly filled with men of lofty intelligence and brilliance; the people’s garments are dyed in five colors, shimmering and magnificent, while the women apply white cosmetics and all wear pearl rings. The land is high and dry, abounding in rare treasures; merchants from the four quarters conduct their trade using gold and silver coins. The five grains are abundant and cheap, so that every household has stores for the future. Along the market stalls, various delicious soups and rice dishes are displayed for sale, so that one may obtain food whenever hungry. For thirst, one drinks grape wine and other blended liquors; the joy is beyond words.
The king of that land was named Milinda; he ruled the country with the True Dharma.

Milinda was a man of high talent and wisdom, well-versed in the worldly scriptures and the Way, capable of debating matters of the past, future, and present. He was proficient in administrative affairs and the arts of warfare, and there were no strategic plans to which his intelligence did not penetrate.
At that time, the king went out of the city for recreation, with his various troops stationed and surrounding him outside.
The king’s mind was filled with self-conceit:
"I am a king; I am able to answer the doctrines of the ninety-six kinds of scriptures."
"The questions people ask him are inexhaustible; as soon as a person’s mind is stirred, he already foreknows what they will say.
The King said to his attendants:
"It is still too early to enter the city, and there is nothing to be done."
"In this realm, is there any monk or śramaṇa who has mastered the scriptures and is able to debate with me regarding the sutras and the Way?
A minister of the king named Tiṃbila-vaṅga addressed the king, saying:
"Indeed, there is."
"There is a śramaṇa named Yaśas who is profoundly enlightened in the scriptures and the Way; he is able to debate with the king and discourse upon the Way.
The king then issued an edict for Jñānagupta to go and invite him to come.
Zhanmiliwangqun immediately went to invite Yehe Luo, saying:
"The Great King wishes to see the Great Master. Yehe Luo replied:
"Very well. If the King wishes to see me, he should come in person; I shall not go to him.
Zhanmilili returned and reported this to the king. The king immediately mounted his carriage and, accompanied by five hundred horsemen, went to the monastery.
When the King met with Yaśas, he greeted him and took his seat; the five hundred horsemen following him all sat down as well.
The King then asked Yaśas:
"For what reason have you abandoned your home and forsaken your wife and children, shaving your head and beard, donning the *kāṣāya*, and becoming a *śramaṇa*?"
"What kind of path do you seek?
Vatsa replied to the king:

"We study the Buddha's path and practice loyalty and integrity; we obtain its blessings in this life and shall obtain its blessings in future lives as well. For this reason, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and become a *śramaṇa*."
The King asked Vatsa:
"If there is a layperson who has a wife and children, and who practices loyalty and righteousness toward his family and children, will he obtain its blessings in this present life?"
"Will they also obtain blessings in future lives? Yasa replied,
"Laypeople who have wives and children at home, yet practice loyalty and integrity, will obtain blessings in this life and will also obtain blessings in future lives."
The king said, "A layperson who has a wife and children at home may practice loyal governance; thus they obtain blessings both in this life and in future lives.
Yet you have abandoned your wife and children for no reason, shaved your head and beard, donned the kāṣāya robe, and become a śramaṇa."
Yasa of the Wild Mango Grove remained silent and had no reply for the king.
A courtier said to him:
"This śramaṇa is greatly enlightened, powerful, and wise; he was merely pressed for time and has not yet had the opportunity to speak."
The king’s attendant minister raised his hand and said:
“Victory to the King! Victory to the King!”
Vatsa remained silent and accepted his defeat.
The king then looked around at the lay followers on his left and right, but the faces of those lay followers showed no sign of shame.
The King thought:
"Even these upāsakas have faces that are difficult to shame; there must be some learned and capable śramaṇas who are able to debate with me!"
The King said to Jianmili: "Is there any other sage of clear wisdom who can engage me in debate and discourse upon the Way?
At that time, Nāgasena, the master of the śramaṇas, was constantly entering and leaving together with the śramaṇas; all the śramaṇas were made to expound the sūtras.

Nāgasena was thoroughly conversant with the essential and difficult points of all the sūtras and was able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Having explained the sūtras through their various distinct sections, chapters, and phrases, he understood the path of Nirvāṇa; none could exhaust his knowledge, and none could surpass him. He was able to resolve all doubts and clarify the thoughts of others. His wisdom was like the rivers and seas, capable of subduing the ninety-six types of heterodox paths. He was revered by the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples and looked up to as a refuge by all the wise; he constantly instructed people in the Way of the sūtras.
Nāgasena arrived in the kingdom of Śāketa, accompanied by disciples who were all exceptionally brilliant. Nāgasena was like a fierce lion.
Jāṇussoni addressed the king, saying:

"There is an extraordinary śramaṇa named Nāgasena; his wisdom is profound and subtle, he clearly understands the essentials of all the sūtras, he can resolve all doubts, there is nothing he does not master, and he is capable of debating the principles of the scriptures with Your Majesty."
The king asked Jñānagupta:
"Are you truly able to undergo hardships together with me for the sake of the Way? Jñānagupta replied:
“Yes, indeed. We are able to debate the sutras and the Way with the King;
we could even debate the sutras and the Way with the seventh Brahmā heaven, let alone with a king of men.”
He then commanded Jāṇussoni to go at once and invite Nātaputta.
Jāṇussoni immediately went to where Nātaputta was and said to him:
"The Great King wishes to see you."
Nāgasena then accompanied his disciples to the king’s presence.
Although the king had never before met Nāgasena, as he stood among the crowd, his attire and gait were so distinct from others that the king recognized him from afar by his demeanor.
The King himself said:
"Among the vast multitudes I have seen before and after, and the great assemblies that have entered this hall, I have never felt such terror as I feel today upon seeing Nāgasena."
"Today Nāgasena will certainly defeat me; I am surely his inferior.
My heart is filled with dread and anxiety.
Jāṇussoni said to the king:
"Nagasena has already arrived outside.
When Nagasena had reached the gate, the King asked Jāṇussoni: "Who is this Nagasena?"
Candimā then pointed him out to the king, who was immediately filled with great joy,
exclaiming, "This is indeed Nāgasena, whom I have been seeking!
The king then observed that Nāgasena’s robes and his manner of walking were utterly distinct from those of the common crowd.
Nāgasena arrived and, having approached to exchange greetings, the King was greatly delighted and they sat down together.
Nāgasena said to the King:

"The Buddhist scriptures state that for a person, peace and security are the greatest benefit; for a person, knowing contentment is the greatest wealth; for a person, having faith is the greatest depth of character; and the path to Nirvāṇa is the greatest bliss."
The king then asked Nāgasena,
"What is your name? Nāgasena replied:
"My parents named me Nāgasena, so people call me Nāgasena.

At times my parents call me Visena, at times they call me Sūrasena, and at times they call me Vijayasena; it is for this reason that everyone knows me by these names, for all people in the world have such names."
The king asked Nāgasena, "Who is this Nāgasena?
The king asked again:
"Is the head Nāgasena? Nāgasena replied, "The head is not Nāgasena."
The king asked again:
"Which is the foremost among the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth? Nāgasena replied:
"The eyes, ears, nose, and mouth are not Nāgasena.
The King asked again:
"Are the neck, shoulders, arms, feet, and hands Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena said, "It was not for Nāgasena.
The king asked again:
"Are the thighs and legs Nāgasena?
Nāgasena replied, "They are not Nāgasena.
The King asked again, "Is the complexion Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena said, "I am not Nāgasena.
The king asked again:
"Are suffering and pleasure Nāgasena?
Nāgasena replied, "They are not Nāgasena."
The King asked again:
"Are good and evil Nāgasena? Nāgasena replied:
"It is not Nāgasena," [the monk replied].
The King asked again:
"Is the body Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena said, "It is not for Nāgasena.
The king asked again:
“Are the liver, lungs, heart, spleen, blood vessels, intestines, and stomach the *nāga*?
Nāgasena replied, “They are not the *nāga*.”
The King asked again:
"Are the complexion, suffering and happiness, good and evil, and the body and mind combined—these five things—to be considered Nāgasena? Nāgasena replied:
"Not Nāgasena," [the monk replied].
The King asked again:
"Suppose there were no physical form, nor suffering or pleasure, nor good or evil, nor body or mind—if these five things were absent, would he still be Nāgasena?"
Nāgasena said, "It was not for Nāgasena.
The king asked again:
"Are the sounds and breaths Nāgasena?
Nāgasena replied, "They are not Nāgasena."
The king asked again,
"Who is this Nāgasena? Nāgasena asked the king in return:
"What constitutes a 'fine carriage' as a carriage?
Is it the axle that constitutes the carriage? The king said:
"The axle does not constitute the chariot.
Nāgasena said: "Is it the rim that constitutes the chariot?"
The King said,
"The rim does not constitute the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Are the spokes the chariot?
The King replied,
"The spokes are not the chariot."
Nāgasena asked, "Is the hub the chariot?
The King replied:
"The hub does not constitute the chariot.
Nāgasena said: "Is it the axle that constitutes the chariot?"
The king said, "The axle is not the chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is the yoke the chariot?
The King replied,
"The yoke is not the chariot."
Nāgasena asked, "Is the carriage the chariot?
The King replied:
"The carriage is not the chariot.
Nāgasena said: "Is the pole the chariot?"
The king said, "A yoke is not a chariot. Nāgasena said:
“Is the canopy the chariot?
The King replied,
“The canopy is not the chariot.”
Nāgasena said: "If one were to gather all these pieces of timber and place them together on one side, would that constitute a chariot?
The King said:
"Even if all these pieces of timber were gathered together and placed on one side, they would not constitute a chariot.
Nāgasena said: "Suppose these pieces of timber were not gathered together; could they then be a chariot?"
The king said:
"It is not appropriate to assemble these various pieces of timber; they do not constitute a chariot. Nāgasena said:
"Is sound the chariot? The king replied,
"Sound is not the chariot."
Nāgasena asked, "What constitutes a chariot?
The king then remained silent and did not speak.
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha’s sūtras explain it thus: just as when these various pieces of wood are assembled together to make a chariot, one obtains what is called a 'chariot' because of them;

so too is it with a person. When the head, face, ears, nose, mouth, neck, shoulders, arms, bones, flesh, hands, feet, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, kidneys, intestines, stomach, complexion, voice, breath, suffering, pleasure, good, and evil are all assembled together, this collection is named a 'person.'"
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Can you debate with me on the difficult points of the sutras? Nāgasena replied,
"If Your Majesty were to engage me in questioning with wisdom, we would be able to debate."
"The King, harboring a sense of pride and nobility, was unable to challenge him.
The King asked Nāgasena,
"What are the characteristics of a wise person?"

Nāgasena said: "The wise man, when engaging in discourse and cross-examination, speaks with mutual understanding, speaks with superior speech, speaks with inferior speech, recognizes victory and defeat, distinguishes between correct and incorrect speech, and knows for himself what is right and wrong; this is the mark of supreme wisdom."
"The wise do not give way to anger; such is the nature of the wise.
The King asked Nāgasena again, "What kind of speech does a king utter?"
Nāgasena said: "A king speaks with total license;
if anyone dares to oppose or disobey his word, the king immediately punishes them by force. Such is the nature of a king's speech."
The King said: "I wish to follow the words of the wise, not the words of a king.

Do not speak to me with the mindset one holds toward a sovereign; rather, when speaking to me, you should speak as you would to the śramaṇas, as you would to my disciples, as you would to the upāsakas, and as you would to the messengers who serve the assembly of śramaṇas. You must not harbor fear, but maintain an utterly upright mind and enlighten me."
Nāgasena said, "Very well. The king said:
"I wish to ask something. Nāgasena said:
"Then let the King ask."
The king said, "I have already asked. Nāgasena replied:
"I have already answered," [the monk said]. The king asked,
"What words did you answer me?"
Nāgasena said: "What words did Your Majesty ask me?
The King replied:
"I have nothing to ask," said Nāgasena.
"I have nothing to answer."
The king thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses great brilliance and profound wisdom.
I shall now begin to question him extensively."
The king thought to himself:
"The sun is about to set; what should I do?
Tomorrow I shall invite Nāgasena to my palace and question him skillfully."
The King said to Tiṣya:
"Tell Nāgasena that it is already dark today; invite him to return to the palace tomorrow, so that we may engage in excellent debate."
Jianmilifangqun then said to Naxian: "The sun is about to set;
Your Majesty should return to the palace.
Tomorrow, Your Majesty intends to invite Naxian."
Nāgasena said, "Very well.
The king then mounted his horse and returned to the palace.
While on horseback, the King continued to think of the name Nāgasena, intending to say "Nāgasena.
Nāgasena thought of him until the next day.
On that morning, Tiṣyarakṣitā, along with the assembly and his ministers, addressed the King, saying:
"Should we indeed invite Nāgasena?
The King replied, "We shall invite him."
Jianmiliwang addressed the assembly, saying,
"How many śramaṇas should the one who requests [the audience] bring with him?
The King replied:
"Nāgasena has come with several śramaṇas.
The king’s treasurer, named Mātsarya, said to the king:
"It would be acceptable to let Nāgasena come together with ten śramaṇas."
The King spoke again:
"I permit Nāgasena to come accompanied by as many śramaṇas as he wishes.
Māka then addressed the King, saying:
"Let Nāgasena come together with ten śramaṇas.
The king spoke again:
"I grant that Nāgasena may come as he pleases, accompanied by however many śramaṇas he wishes."
Māluṅkyāputta spoke again to the king:
"It will be acceptable only if Nāgasena comes together with ten other śramaṇas.
When the king heard Māluṅkyāputta’s mention of such a large number, he became enraged at Māluṅkyāputta.
"You are truly a peerless miser.
Your very name is 'Miser. You do not even hope for the King's property; as for your own possessions, how could you possibly cherish them?
Since you do not know how to oppose my will, you shall incur the punishment of execution."
The king said, "You may go;
I pity you and pardon your offense. Now that I have become king, am I unable to provide a meal for a śramaṇa?
The stingy man was filled with shame and did not dare speak again.
Chenmiliwangqun immediately went to where Nāgasena was, approached him, paid his respects, and said:
"The Great King invites Nāgasena. Nāgasena replied:
"Your Majesty, how many śramaṇas should I be permitted to accompany me?
Jñānagiri looked toward the assembly and said,
"The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya wishes to go accompanied by how many śramaṇas?"
Nāgasena then set out together with eighty śramaṇas, including Vatsīputra and others.
Candimā and his followers all accompanied them, intending to enter the city at dawn.
Tianmili Wangqun and the others among the assembly all asked Nāgasena:
"Yesterday you told the King that [the soul] does not exist;
why then do you claim to be Nāgasena? Nāgasena then asked Tianmili Wangqun:
"What do you mean by 'Nāgasena'? Cāmali, looking toward the assembly, replied:
"I take the breath that enters and exits—the vital life-force—to be Nāgasena."
Nāgasena asked Caṇḍagirika:
"If a person's breath once departs and does not return, will that person ever be born again? Caṇḍagirika replied:
"When the breath goes out and does not return, it is certain that death has occurred. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a person blowing a flute; once the breath has gone out, it does not enter back in again."
"It is like a person holding a gold-smith's bellows to blow a fire; once the breath has issued forth, can it ever return back inside?
Jāmbūnada said, "It cannot return."
“It is like a person blowing into the earth with a horn; when the breath has once gone out, does it ever return back in?
Jāṃbūnada said: “It does not return.”
Nāgasena said: "If the vital breaths once gone out do not return, why does a person not die?
Caṇḍagirika replied: "Because..."
"In the intervals between our breaths, we cannot know [this]; we pray that you will explain it for us.
Nāgasena said: "The breath of inhalation and exhalation are all matters pertaining to the body."
When a person has something in mind, the tongue speaks it out; this is the function of the tongue.
When there is something the mind suspects, the heart reflects upon it; this is the function of the mind.
"Each has its own master; when examined individually, all are empty, and there is no Na-xian.
When Zhānmílì saw that the minds of the assembly were thus opened and liberated, he immediately received the five precepts and became an upāsaka.
Nāgasena then proceeded forward into the palace, reached the king’s presence, and ascended the throne hall. The king immediately paid homage to Nāgasena and withdrew.
Nāgasena then took his seat, and all eighty śramaṇas sat down together with him.
The king prepared an exquisite meal and personally served it first to the śramaṇa Nāgasena.

When the meal was finished and the king had completed washing his hands, he bestowed upon each of the other śramaṇas a single undergarment (nivasana) and a pair of leather sandals; to Nāgasena and to Yaśoda, he gave three robes each and a pair of leather sandals each.
The King said to Nāgasena and Yaśas:
"Let ten men remain together and send the others away.
Nāgasena immediately sent the other śramaṇas away and kept ten men together.
The King commanded the ladies of the inner palace and the court musicians and dancers:
"All of you shall remain within the curtains on the palace floor and listen as I engage in debate on the Way with Nāgasena.
Thereupon, the ladies and musicians all emerged from behind the curtains on the palace floor to listen to Nāgasena’s exposition of the sutras.
Then the king took his seat before Nāgasena and said,
"What should be spoken of? Nāgasena replied:
"If Your Majesty wishes to hear the essential words, I shall speak those essential words. The King said,
"What do you all consider to be the most essential?"
"For what purpose do you practice as śramaṇas?
Nāgasena replied, "We wish to abandon the hardships of this world and do not wish to undergo the hardships of future lives; for this reason, we practice as śramaṇas."
"We consider this to be the most essential good.
The King asked,
"Do all these śramaṇas become śramaṇas because they do not wish to undergo further hardship in this life or in future lives?"
Nāgasena said: "It is not for all these reasons alone that one becomes a śramaṇa.
There are four classes of śramaṇas."
The king asked, "What are these four? Nāgasena replied:

"Among them, some become śramaṇas because they owe debts; some become śramaṇas because they fear government officials; some become śramaṇas because they are impoverished; and some become śramaṇas because they truly desire to abandon the sufferings of this world and the next."
Nāgasena said, "I originally became a śramaṇa because I sought the Way with a sincere heart. The King said:
"Now, do you practice the Way because you have become a śramaṇa?
Nāgasena replied,
"I became a śramaṇa when I was young."
There is the Buddha’s sutras and the Way, as well as his disciples; among all the śramaṇas, many are highly enlightened and wise.
Having studied the sutras and precepts under them, they have entered my heart. For this reason, I have abandoned the sufferings of both this life and future lives and have become a śramaṇa.
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked:
"Is there anyone who, after death, is not reborn? Nāgasena replied:
"Among those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), some are reborn in a future life; others are not reborn."
The King asked:
"Who is it that will be born in future lives?
Who is it that will not be born again?"
Nāgasena said: "If a person possesses affection and craving, they will be reborn in the next world;
if a person lacks affection and craving, they will not be reborn in the next world."
The king asked, "If a person,
with a single-minded thought, contemplates the True Dharma and performs good deeds, will they not be reborn in future lives?
Nāgasena replied:
"Because a person recollects the True Dharma with a single-minded focus, recollects wholesome wisdom, and other wholesome matters, they will not be reborn in future lives.
The King asked:
"When a person recollects the True Dharma, goodness, and wisdom with a single-minded focus, are the meanings of these two things—the same or not?"
Nāgasena said, "Their meanings are each distinct and not the same.
The king asked Nāgasena:
"Are oxen, horses, and the six domestic animals somewhat intelligent, or are they without intelligence?
Nāgasena replied, "Oxen, horses, and the six domestic animals each possess their own intelligence; it is simply that their minds differ."
Nāgasena said: "Has Your Majesty ever seen those harvesting wheat?
They hold the wheat in their left hand and cut it with their right."
Nāgasena said, “A person of wisdom cuts off craving and desire, just as one reaps wheat.
The King said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What are those other virtuous deeds?"
Nāgasena said, "Sincerity and faith,
filial piety and obedience, diligence and mindfulness of the good, single-mindedness, and wisdom— these constitute wholesome deeds.
The King said:
“What is meant by one who possesses sincerity and faith? Nāgasena replied:

“One who possesses sincerity and faith has no further doubts; they believe that there is a Buddha, they believe in the Buddha’s teachings and the Dharma, they believe in the Saṃgha of monks, they believe in the existence of Arhats, they believe in this present life, they believe in future lives, they believe in filial piety toward one’s parents, and they believe that performing good deeds results in good retribution, while performing evil deeds results in evil retribution.”
Having attained faith, the subsequent mind becomes pure, and one immediately departs from and leaves behind the five evils.
What are these five evils?
First, lustful desire; second, anger and hatred; third, drowsiness and sleep; fourth, frivolous amusement; and fifth, doubt.
"If one does not abandon these five evils, the mind will remain unsettled;
if one abandons these five evils, the mind will become pure. Nāgasena said:
"It is like this: Suppose a Cakravartin King, with his chariots, horses, and retinue, crosses a river by wading through it, making the water turbid and foul.
Once he has crossed over and gone on his way, the King becomes thirsty and wishes to drink water."
The king possesses a water-clearing jewel; when it is placed in turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear, and the king can then drink the pure water.
Nāgasena said, “When the human mind harbors evil, it is like turbid water.”
The disciples of the Buddha have attained the path that transcends birth and death; their minds are pure, like a pearl in clear water.
When people repel all evils and possess sincere faith and purity, they are like the bright moon-jewel.
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked:
"What is meant by 'a person who is diligent and sincere'? Nāgasena replied:

"Among the disciples of the Buddha, when they see one another, they cast off all evil thoughts. Among them, some attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, some attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some attain the stage of *anāgāmin*, and some attain the stage of *arhat*. Furthermore, those who, following one another's example, practice with sincerity and faith, all likewise attain the path that transcends the world."

Nāgasena said: "Suppose it were raining heavily on a mountain and the water flowed down in a vast torrent; people on both banks would not know the depth of the water and, fearing it, would not dare to cross."

It is like a person from a distant land who comes to look at water; though they do not see it directly, they know whether the water is wide or narrow, deep or shallow, and knowing their own strength and capacity to enter the water, they are able to cross over.
The crowds on both sides followed their example and subsequently also succeeded in crossing over.

It is the same for the Buddha’s disciples: seeing that those before them attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat* through the purification of their minds, all realize these states through the power of a virtuous mind and diligent effort.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
A person who possesses a heart of sincerity and faith can attain liberation from the world by themselves.
Only a practitioner who is able to restrain and reject the five desires and recognizes the suffering inherent in the body can achieve liberation from the world.
"All people achieve their virtue and morality through wisdom.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked,
"What constitutes filial piety? Nāgasena replied:
"All who are virtuous are filial and obedient.
Indeed, all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment take filial piety as their foundation.
The King said:
"What are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? Nāgasena replied:
"There are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path."
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
Nāgasena replied to the King:

“The Buddha has taught: first, the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body; second, the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings; third, the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the mind as the mind; and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating phenomena as phenomena.”
"These are the four foundations of mindfulness.
The king spoke again:
"What are the four right efforts?"
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha taught that having already analyzed and ceased four matters, one no longer dwells upon them; this is called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
By attaining the four right efforts, one then naturally attains the mindfulness of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)."
The King asked again,
"What are the four foundations of miraculous power? Nāgasena replied:
"First, the eyes can see through; second, the ears can hear through; third, one can know what is being thought in the minds of others; fourth, the body can fly."
"These are the four bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) regarding mindfulness.
The King asked again:
"What are the five faculties (indriya)?"

Nāgasena said: "First, when the eye sees beautiful or ugly forms, the mind does not become attached; this is a faculty. Second, when the ear hears pleasant sounds or harsh abuse, the mind does not become attached; this is a faculty. Third, when the nose smells fragrances or foul odors, the mind does not become attached; this is a faculty. Fourth, when the mouth encounters delicious flavors or bitter and pungent tastes, the mind does not become attached; this is a faculty. Fifth, when the body encounters what is smooth and delicate, the mind feels no joy, and when it encounters what is coarse and hard, the mind feels no aversion; these are the five faculties."
The King asked again:
"What are the five powers? Nāgasena replied:

"First, the power to restrain the eye; second, the power to restrain the ear; third, the power to restrain the nose; fourth, the power to restrain the mouth; fifth, the power to restrain the body so that the mind does not fall [into error]. These are the five powers."
The king asked again:
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment?
Nāgasena replied:

1. The awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), 2. the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga), 3. the awakening factor of energy (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga), 4. the awakening factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga), 5. the awakening factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), 6. the awakening factor of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), and 7. the awakening factor of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga).
"These are the seven factors of enlightenment.
The king asked again:
"What are the eightfold path of practice?"
Nāgasena said: "First, right view;
second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration."
"These are the eightfold path of practice.
All thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are fundamentally rooted in filial piety. Nāgasena said:

“Ordinary people who carry heavy loads over long distances and achieve their goals do so entirely because of the earth; the five grains, trees, and plants that look toward the heavens in this world all grow from the earth.”
Nāgasena said: "It is like a master builder who, intending to construct a great city, must first measure out and lay the foundation before he can erect the city.
Nāgasena continued:

"Just as a performer who wishes to perform must first clear and level the ground before performing, so too a disciple of the Buddha seeking the Way must first practice the sutras and precepts, contemplate the causes of goodness, and understand the nature of diligent effort and suffering; only then can they abandon all cravings and desires and contemplate the eightfold path."
The king asked,
"What should one employ to cast off all cravings?
Nāgasena replied:
"By single-mindedly contemplating the Way, craving and desire will naturally cease.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked again,
"What is it to be diligent? Nāgasena replied:
"To uphold what is wholesome and assist in what is wholesome is called diligence. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a wall that is about to collapse; one props it up from the side."
"To prop up a house that is collapsing and about to fall is what is called diligence. Nāgasena said:

"It is like a king who dispatches his troops to launch an attack; if the troops are weak and about to be defeated, the king dispatches further troops to assist them, and the troops then achieve victory."
When a person possesses various evils, it is like being few and weak in the face of an army;
when a person maintains a virtuous mind to extinguish an evil mind, it is like a king increasing his troops and achieving victory.
Maintaining the five virtuous minds to eliminate the five evil minds is like winning a battle.
"This is what constitutes diligence as an aid to the wholesome.
It is thus," Nāgasena said.
“Supported by diligence, once one has led others to the path of goodness, they shall attain the path that transcends the world, from which there is no returning.
The King said: “Excellent!”
The King asked again:
"What is meant by 'the mind should contemplate all wholesome things'?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is like a person who takes various kinds of flowers and binds them together with thread; even if the wind blows, they cannot be scattered.
Nāgasena spoke again:
"It is like a king’s treasurer, who knows the quantity of gold, silver, pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, and precious jewels within the royal treasury."

When a practitioner of the Way desires to attain the Way, they bring to mind the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; this is precisely what is meant by "mindfulness of the path that transcends the world."

When a person possesses the intention for the Way, they thereby come to know good and evil; knowing what ought to be practiced and what ought not to be practiced, they distinguish between the white and the black. After reflecting within themselves, they then abandon evil and pursue good.

Nāgasena said: "It is like a king who has a gatekeeper; he knows those whom the king respects and those whom the king does not respect; he knows those who benefit the king and those who do not benefit the king."

The gatekeeper knows those whom the king honors and those who benefit the king, and he admits them; he knows those whom the king does not honor and those who do not benefit the king, and the gatekeeper does not admit them.
Nāgasena said: "A person who maintains their mind is just like this: one should internalize all that is wholesome and not internalize what is unwholesome.
Guarding the mind and restraining the heart is also analogous to this."
Nāgasena spoke in a sutra, saying:
"A person should firmly guard their own mind and the six objects of desire within the body; by holding the mind with firm resolve, one shall naturally attain the time of transcending the world."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena:
"What is that one thing which is the mind? Nāgasena replied:
"Among all virtues, the single-mindedness of the mind alone is supreme; if a person can unify their mind, all virtues will follow it."

Nāgasena said: "It is like a multi-storied building or a staircase which must have something to lean upon; likewise, all those who perform wholesome deeds fix their minds upon a single point. Nāgasena said:

"It is, for example, like a king who sets out for battle with his fourfold army; the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry all lead and follow the king from front and rear."
The Buddha’s various sutras, precepts, and other virtuous deeds all follow from a single mind, just as, for example, soldiers [follow a general].
Nāgasena spoke in the sutra, saying:
"Among all virtues, a single mind is the foundation; though there are many practitioners of the Way, they should all first return to a single mind."
"The birth and death of human beings pass away like water flowing downstream; preceding and succeeding moments follow one another without a moment of abiding.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked again:
"Who is a wise person? Nāgasena replied:
"I have already said before that when a person possesses wisdom, they are able to sever all doubts and clarify all wholesome matters; this is what constitutes wisdom.
Nāgasena replied, "It is like taking a lamp into a dark room: as soon as the lamp enters the room, it dispels the darkness and illuminates itself."
"A person who possesses wisdom is like the light of a fire. Nāgasena said,
"It is like a person holding a sharp knife to cut wood."
"A person with wisdom can sever all evils, just as a sharp blade does. Nāgasena said:
"In this world, wisdom is the foremost of all things."
"If a person possesses wisdom, they can attain liberation from the suffering of birth and death.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King said:
"Nāgasena, since the various sūtras you have previously spoken differ from one another, do they not merely intend to eliminate all evil?
Nāgasena replied:
"Indeed. The various kinds of goodness spoken of in the Buddha's sutras are intended solely to eliminate all evils. Nāgasena said:
"Just as when a king dispatches his fourfold army, although they engage in battle, at the time of their initial dispatch his intention is merely to attack the enemy;
so too, the various virtues taught in the sūtras spoken by the Buddha are intended solely to join forces in attacking and removing all evil."
The king said: "Excellent, excellent!
Nāgasena’s exposition of the sūtra is most delightful."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person dies and proceeds along the path of good or evil, does the spirit of the old body continue its activity to take birth,
or does it take birth by means of another spirit?"
Nāgasena said: "It is neither the same as the former body and spirit, nor is it separate from the former body and spirit.
Nāgasena then asked:
“O King, when you were small and nursing at the breast, was that body the same as the body you have now upon reaching adulthood?
The King replied,
“The body of my childhood was different.”
Nāgasena said: "When a person is in the mother’s womb, at the very moment the semen first enters and while it is still turbid, is that [person] the semen?
"No, it is different."
“When they were firm as flesh and bone, was it that same semen? “It was different.
“From the time of birth until the age of several years, was it that same semen?”
“It is different. “Suppose a person is practicing calligraphy; can a bystander possibly take over their skill for them?
The King said:
"One cannot substitute for another's labor. Nāgasena said:
"Suppose a person commits a crime and is guilty; could one take an innocent person to substitute for him?"
The king said, "It is not so.
Nāgasena spoke to the king concerning the spirit and the nature of demerit, but the king’s mind did not understand; therefore, the king said:
"If someone were to ask Nāgasena, how would Nāgasena explain it? Nāgasena replied:
"It is simply this body from when I was small; from childhood to adulthood, it is the same body that continues."
"When one is large and when one is small, they are contained within a single body for nourishment; this is what life sustains.
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person lights a lamp; will it not continue until daybreak?"
The king said,
"The oil lamp will burn until dawn. Nāgasena said:
"Does the flame of the lamp not persist because the wick and fire continue throughout the night?
Does the flame of the lamp not persist because they continue until midnight?
Does the flame of the lamp not persist because they continue until dawn?"
The king said, "This is not the light of a fire. Nāgasena said:
“Did Dīpaṃkara light the lamps again from the first watch of the night until midnight?
And did he light them again at the time of dawn?
The king said:
"It is not that the fire is lit again at midnight; rather, because the flame continues, a single wick of fire lasts until dawn. Nāgasena said:
"The succession of a person's spirit is also like this: as one [moment] passes, another arrives."

A person arises from the spirit; after reaching old age and death, the spirit proceeds further toward its destination of rebirth, continuing in a revolving succession. Thus, while this [new] spirit is not the same as the former spirit, it is also not separate from the former spirit.
"After a person dies, the spirit then has a destination where it is born. Nāgasena said:
"Suppose milk curdles into curds; from the curds, one takes the cream and boils it to produce ghee. Could one take that ghee and the cream from the curds and call it 'milk' again?"
"Can the words of that man be trusted?
The King replied,
"The words of that man cannot be trusted."
Nāgasena said: "Just as milk turns into curd, curd into whey, and whey into clarified butter (ghṛta), so too it is with the human spirit:

from the spirit comes birth; from birth to growth; from growth to old age; and from old age to death. After death, the spirit undergoes birth once more; when one body dies, one must again receive another body."
"It is like two lamps illuminating one another.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If there is a person who will not be reborn in a future life, can that person know it for themselves?
Nāgasena replied:
"Indeed. There are those who are able to know it for themselves.
The king said:
"How is this known? Nāgasena replied:

"That person knows for themselves that they are free from affection, free from craving, and free from all evil deeds; therefore, they know for themselves that they will not be reborn in future lives."

Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose there is a farmer who plows his fields and sows grain, harvesting a great deal and storing it in his granary; then, in the following year, he no longer plows nor sows, but relies solely on the grain in his granary for food."
"Would that farmer ever expect to obtain new grain again?
The King replied, "He has no expectation whatsoever."
Nāgasena said, "How does that farmer know that he will not obtain grain again?
The King asked:
"Since that farming household no longer plows nor sows, they have nothing to hope for.
Nāgasena said: "Attaining the Way is also like this;

one knows for oneself that one has already cast off affection, love, suffering, and pleasure, and possesses no greedy mind. For this reason, one knows for oneself that one will not be born again in future lives."
The king spoke again:
"If that person will not be reborn in future lives, does he now possess any wisdom that differs from that of ordinary people?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is so. His wisdom is different from that of ordinary men.
The King said:
"Could there possibly be light? Nāgasena replied, "Yes."
"There is clarity.
The King asked:
"Is there a difference or similarity between wisdom and clarity?"
Nāgasena said, "Wisdom and clarity are one and the same.
The King asked:
"Does one who possesses the clarity of wisdom know all things completely, or is there something they do not know?
Nāgasena replied:
“Human intelligence has its reach and its limits. The King asked,
“In what way does human intelligence have its reach and its limits?”
Nāgasena said: "What a person has not previously studied, they do not previously know;
what a person has previously studied, they previously know."
When the wise perceive people and all things, they see that all must pass away and return to emptiness, lacking any autonomy.
That which the human mind covets and delights in is entirely the root of suffering; from this, suffering arises.
"The wise know that matters of success and failure are impermanent; this wisdom is what distinguishes them from others.
The King asked, "When a person possesses wisdom, where does their folly reside?"
Nāgasena said: "When a person possesses wisdom, all forms of folly are naturally extinguished. Nāgasena said:
"Just as when a person enters a dark room carrying a lamp, the room becomes entirely bright and the darkness is instantly extinguished;
so it is with wisdom: when a person possesses wisdom, all ignorance and folly are completely extinguished."
The king asked, "Where is human wisdom now? Nāgasena replied:
“When a person practices wisdom, that wisdom subsequently ceases; yet what was accomplished by wisdom remains as an action. Nāgasena said:
“It is like a person who writes characters by the light of a fire at night; when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain.”
"In this way, O Wise One, once that which is to be accomplished has been achieved, the wisdom itself ceases, while what was accomplished remains.
The King said: "That wisdom should cease of its own accord once it has accomplished its task—what kind of statement is this?"
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person who prepares five jars of water as a precaution against fire.
If a fire should break out, that person takes the five jars of water and sprinkles them to extinguish the fire."
"After the fire has been extinguished, would that person who rescued it from the flames still hope to recover the intact jar and take it home?
The King said, "That person would no longer have such hope; since the jar is broken and the fire extinguished, how could he still hope for the jar?"
Nāgasena said: "A practitioner of the Way maintains the five wholesome minds to extinguish all evils, just as water in a jar extinguishes fire.
The King said:
"What are the five virtues? Nāgasena replied:

"First, faith that there is good and evil; second, not disparaging the sūtras or the precepts; third, diligence; fourth, possessing wisdom and mindfulness of the good; fifth, single-mindedly recollecting the Path—these are the five virtues."

If a person can practice these five virtues, they will attain wisdom; they will know that the body and all phenomena are impermanent; they will know that there is suffering and no self-mastery; and they will know that all is empty and devoid of inherent existence.
Nāgasena said: "Suppose a physician takes five kinds of medicine to a patient's house and gives the medicine to the patient to drink.
Once the patient has drunk the medicine and is cured, would the physician expect to get the same medicine back to treat another person?"
The king said, “I no longer hope to obtain the old medicine. Nāgasena said:
"The five kinds of medicine are like the five types of wholesome wisdom.
The physician is like the seeker of the Way.
The patient is like all manner of evils."
The ignorant are like the sick;
those who have attained the Way and crossed over the world are like those whose illness has been cured.
That which is accomplished through wisdom is the path by which people cross over the world.
"Once a person has attained the Way, their wisdom also ceases of its own accord. Nāgasena said:

"Suppose a skilled warrior takes up his bow and arrows and advances toward the enemy; having shot five arrows at the foe and achieved victory, would that man ever expect those arrows to return back to him?"
The king said, "I no longer hope for the arrow. Nāgasena said:
"The five arrows" refers to the five kinds of knowledge possessed by humans.
A wise person attains the Way through wisdom, just as a valiant warrior conquers his enemies in battle.
"All evils" refers to all manner of evils.
The practitioner of the Way maintains the five wholesome minds to extinguish all evils; when all evils are extinguished, wholesome wisdom immediately arises.
By means of this wholesome wisdom, a person attains deliverance from the world, for the Way is eternally present and never ceases.
The king said, “Excellent! The king said:
“If a person has attained the Way and will not be born again in future lives, will they still experience suffering again?
Nāgasena replied: “Some may experience further suffering, while others may not.”
The king asked,
"What is meant by 'further suffering' and 'no further suffering'? Nāgasena replied:
"The body alone experiences suffering; the mind does not experience suffering.
The King asked, "In what way does the body experience suffering while the mind does not?"
Nāgasena said: "The reason the body undergoes further suffering is that the body still exists; therefore, it undergoes further suffering.
When the mind abandons all evils and is free from all desires, for this reason it no longer undergoes further suffering."
The king said:
"If one who has attained the Way of the person is still unable to be free from bodily suffering, does this mean he has not yet attained the Way of Nirvāṇa?
The king asked.
“Once a person has attained the Way, they have no more attachments or loves; their body may suffer, but their mind is at peace. What use, then, is attaining the Way?
The King said, “Suppose a person has already attained the Way and become perfected—what would remain for them to stay for?”
Nāgasena said: "It is like fruit that is not yet ripe; one does not force it to ripen.
Once it is ripe, there is nothing further to wait for."
Nāgasena said: "Your Majesty, as for what you have just mentioned regarding Śariputra—when Śariputra was alive, he said:
'I do not seek death, nor do I seek life; I simply require the proper time. When that time arrives, I shall depart.'"
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!
