Translator’s name lost; appended to the Eastern Jin Records. The King asked:
"Is it good for a person to experience pleasure? Or is it not good? Is it good for a person to experience suffering?"
Is it not so? It is unwholesome.
For the Buddha, there is nothing he does not declare as either pleasant or painful.
The king said, "If conditioned phenomena were non-existent,
there would be no suffering. Nāgasena asked the king:
“Suppose a person were to place a heated iron in their hand; would it not burn the person’s hand?
Furthermore, suppose they were to take ice and place it in their hand; would that ice also burn the person’s hand?”
The King said, "Indeed.
Both hands are majestic."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Are the objects in both hands equally hot?
The king replied:
"Not both hot," said Nāgasena.
"Then are they both cold?"
The King said: "It is not that both are cold. Nāgasena said:
"Both hands are burning. Nāgasena said: "I ask the King again:
if both your hands were heated at different times, one before and one after, you would have to say that both are heated."
"If both are cold, one should say they are both cold.
For what reason could one that is cold and one that is hot be said alike to burn the hand?
The King said:
"My wisdom and discernment are very shallow and limited; I am unable to reach the depth of this difficult question.
I pray that Nāgasena will explain it for me. Nāgasena said:

“The Buddhist scriptures state that there are six things that cause internal joy, six things that cause internal sorrow, another six things that cause neither joy nor sorrow, and furthermore, six external things that cause sorrow.”
The King asked,
"What are the six things that cause a person to rejoice within?
Nāgasena replied:
"First, when the eyes see something and yet have further expectations, this causes one to rejoice within;
second, when the ears hear pleasant sounds and yet have further expectations, this causes one to rejoice within;
third, when the nose smells pleasant fragrances and yet has further expectations, this causes one to rejoice within."
Fourth, when the tongue obtains delicious flavors, there is further expectation; therefore, it causes internal joy.
Fifth, when the body obtains fine and smooth sensations, there is further expectation; therefore, it causes internal joy.
Sixth, when the mind experiences pleasant feelings, there is further expectation; therefore, it causes internal joy.
"These six matters cause people to rejoice within.
The King asked again:
"What are the six external matters that cause people to rejoice?"

Nāgasena said: "First, when one sees beautiful forms with the eye, one reflects that they cannot be obtained forever and must all be abandoned; thus one contemplates for oneself that this is truly impermanent, and for this reason it causes outward joy.
Second, when one hears pleasant sounds with the ear, one reflects that they cannot be obtained forever and must all be abandoned; for this reason it causes outward joy."

Third, when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, one reflects that it cannot be obtained constantly and that all such things must be abandoned; for this reason, it causes people to experience outward joy.

Fourth, when the mouth obtains delicious flavors, one reflects that they cannot be obtained constantly and that all such things must be abandoned; for this reason, it causes people to experience outward joy.

Fifth, when the body obtains smooth and delicate sensations, one reflects that they cannot be obtained constantly and that all such things must be abandoned; for this reason, it causes people to experience outward joy.

Sixth, when one contemplates sensual desires with the mind and reflects that they are all impermanent and must all be abandoned, one feels joy thereafter; these are the six matters that cause a person to feel external joy.
The King asked again:
"What are the six internal matters that cause internal sorrow for a person?
Nāgasena replied:
"First, that which causes internal distress: seeing what is unpleasant to the eyes causes internal distress;
second, hearing what one does not wish to hear causes internal distress;
third, smelling what one does not wish to smell causes internal distress."
Fourth, when one obtains that which the mouth does not desire, it causes inner distress;
fifth, when one wears that which the body does not desire, it causes inner distress;
sixth, when one possesses that which the mind does not find pleasing, it causes inner distress.
"These are the six matters that cause inner sorrow within a person.
The King asked again:
"What are the six external matters that cause a person to be unhappy?"
Nāgasena said: "The first is seeing unpleasant forms with the eyes, which causes people displeasure;
the second is hearing unpleasant sounds with the ears, which causes people displeasure."
Third, the nose smells a foul or fishy odor that causes displeasure;
fourth, the tongue encounters bitterness or pungency that causes displeasure;
fifth, the body comes into contact with coarse or hard textures that cause displeasure.
"Sixth, when the mind harbors hatred, it causes others to be displeased.
These are the six external matters that cause others to be displeased.
The King asked again:
"What are the six things that cause a person neither sorrow nor joy?
Nāgasena replied:
"First, when the eyes see something, one feels neither joy nor sorrow."
Second, when the ear hears sounds, one is neither joyful nor distressed;
third, when the nose smells odors, one is neither joyful nor distressed;
fourth, when the mouth obtains tastes, one is neither joyful nor distressed.
Fifth, when the body encounters contact, one is neither elated nor distressed;
sixth, when the mind entertains thoughts, one is neither elated nor distressed.
These are the six internal matters that cause a person to be neither elated nor distressed.
The King asked again:
"What are the six external things that cause people to grieve?
Nāgasena replied:
"First, when one sees a dead person with one's own eyes, one reflects upon the impermanence of one's own body and all things; that person thinks to themselves:
'I have this realization, so why am I unable to attain the Way?'"
Second, due to external grief, one's ears do not delight in pleasant sounds; such a person thinks to themselves:
"I have these thoughts, so why am I unable to attain the Way?"
Third, because of external grief:
the nose finds neither pleasant nor foul odors agreeable, and the person thinks to themselves, "I have this thought; why is it that I do not attain the Way?"
Fourth, because of external grief, one’s mouth does not perceive the flavors of bitterness or sweetness; the person thinks to themselves:
"I have this thought, so why do I not obtain it?"
The Way is hindered by external anxieties.
Fifth, the body finds neither the pleasantness of the fine and smooth nor the coarseness of the rough and hard; such a person thinks to themselves:
"I have these thoughts, so why am I unable to attain the Way?"
Sixth, due to external grief, the mind harbors no fond desire; the person thinks to themselves:
"I have this thought, yet why is it that I do not attain the Way?"
"External grief arises from these causes;
these are the six matters that cause people external grief.
The King said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"After a person has died, who is it that is reborn in a future life?"
Nāgasena said: "Name and body are reborn in future lives.
The king asked Nāgasena:
“Is it then that a person’s body and conduct arise? Nāgasena replied, “No.”
"It is neither because of the name nor because of the body that one performs good or evil deeds in this present life and is subsequently born in a future life.
The King said:

"If it were the case that one performs good or evil deeds with this present name-body, yet no further body were to arise in a future life, then it would be most excellent to perform good and evil; one could directly attain liberation and never again undergo various sufferings?"
Nāgasena said: "If one performs good deeds in this life and is not reborn in the next, then one may indeed attain liberation.
However, as long as a person does not cease performing both good and evil deeds, they will certainly be reborn in the future; therefore, liberation cannot be attained."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a person steals another's fruit or melons. The owner catches the thief and brings him before the king, saying:
'This man has stolen my fruit.'"
The thief said, "I did not steal this man's fruit; he planted only small seedlings, and originally did not plant fruit.
I took the fruit myself; why should I be considered a thief?"
"I did not steal this person's fruit; therefore, I should not be guilty of an offense.
Nāgasena asked the king, "In such a dispute between these two people, who is the one in the right and who is the one not in the right?"
The king said, "The owner of the plantation is in the right, for he is the original planter.
The thief is without justification and should be held guilty."
Nāgasena said: "Why is it that stealing constitutes an offense?
The King replied:
"Therefore, the thief is guilty because the fruit exists only because it was produced from the roots planted by the original owner. Nāgasena said: "The birth of a person is also like this.
A person performs good or evil deeds in this life using this name-and-body (nāma-rūpa), and thus is born in a future life; those who perform good or evil in this life are the 'original' cause."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a person steals another's grain stalks, and the owner catches him and leads him away, questioning him:
'Why did you steal my grain stalks?'"
The thief said: "I did not steal your grain stalks.
You planted the rice yourself; I simply took the stalks."
"Why should I have committed theft?
The two men led each other before the king and spoke thus: "Which of us is in the right, and which is in the wrong?
The king said:
"To plant grain is upright; to steal it is not upright.
Nāgasena said: "How do you know that one who steals ears of grain is not upright?"
The King said:
"Those who plant rice are the basis; those who do not plant rice have none. On what basis, then, could there be ears of grain?
Nāgasena replied:
"Human life is also like this: in this present life, a person uses this name-body to perform good and evil deeds, which then leads to birth in a future life.
That which performs good and evil in the present life is its very basis."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a person in the cold of winter lights a fire in a house to warm himself.
That person abandons the fire and departs; gradually it spreads to the walls and earth, burning the house and extending to the multi-storied building."
The householder, because of these words, led the one who had started the fire before the king and said:
"This man set the fire, which spread until it burned my towered house.
Then the one who had lit the fire said:
"I merely lit a small fire to warm myself; I did not burn the palace.
Nāgasena asked the king, "Who was telling the truth?"
The King said:
"It is the one who originally kindled the fire that is at fault;
it was produced by him. Nāgasena said:
"Human life is also like this. For example,
just as a person uses this name-body (*nāmakāya*) in the present life to perform good or evil deeds and is thereby born in a future life,
those who perform good or evil deeds in the present life constitute the basis."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a person were to light a candle at night and place it against a wall, intending to use its light to eat his meal.
If the candle were to lean slightly back and touch the wall, the bamboo, the wood, or the timber, it would set the entire house on fire."
The fire blazed fiercely, spreading until it consumed an entire city.
All the people within the city cried out together, saying:
"Why have you burned this entire city to such an extent?"
The one who had lit the fire said:
"I merely lit a small candle flame to illuminate my own meal;
this great fire is not my fire."
Thus they began to dispute and litigate, dragging each other before the king.
Nāgasena asked the king, "In such a case,
who is the one who is right and who is the one who is wrong?"
The King said,
"The one who lights the fire is not upright. Nāgasena said:
"How do you know this?
The king replied,
"It was originally produced by fire."
"Have you finished your meal? You ought to extinguish the fire, lest it burn down the entire city.
Nāgasena said, "The life of a human being is also like this."
In this present life, people perform good and evil through this so-called "name-body," and thereby they are born into future lives.
That which performs good and evil in the present life is its very root.
Because people do not understand how to perform good and evil [properly], they are unable to attain liberation.
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, a man were to betroth money as a gift to request a young girl from another family.
Later, when the girl has grown up, another person again requests her hand in marriage, and the girl is obtained to become his wife."
The family from which she was previously betrothed came and said of themselves,
"Why have you taken her as your wife in defiance?
Then the other family said:
"You took a wife when you were young, while I have taken a wife when I am grown; why should I take your wife as my infant?
Thus they led each other before the king.
Nāgasena said: "O King!
In such a case, who is the one who is right and who is the one who is not right?"
The King said,
"The previous marriage was for a price. Nāgasena said:
"How do you know this? the king asked.
The man replied, "This girl was originally small, but now she has gradually grown up; for this reason, I know she is upright, as she was previously the wife of the man to whom she was betrothed."
Nāgasena said: "The birth of a human being is also like this.
A person performs good or evil deeds in this life by means of this name-body, and thereby takes birth in a future life."
"The performance of good and evil in this present life is its very basis. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a person who takes a vessel and buys fresh milk from a cowherd; having obtained the milk, he returns it to the owner and says:"
"I shall return before long.
After a short while, the man returned to take the milk, but the milk had already turned into curd.
The owner of the milk shop said:
"I entrusted you with milk, yet now you bring me back curd.
The cowherd replied, "This was your original milk; it has simply transformed into curd on its own."
"The two men then began to dispute with one another and, pulling each other along,
went before the king. Nāgasena asked the king,
"In such a case, who is the one in the right?"
The king said,
"The cowherd's family is the rightful owner. Nāgasena said:
"How do you know this, Your Majesty?
The king replied, "You yourself bought some milk and set it down on the ground; it spontaneously turned into curd."
"What fault would there be for a cowherd?
Nāgasena replied, "The life of a human being is also like this."
"In this present life, a person performs good or evil by means of this 'name-body' (nāmakāya), and consequently is born in a future life.
That which performs good or evil in the present life is its very basis.
The King asked again:
"Now, will Nāgasena be reborn again in a future life?
Nāgasena replied to the king:
"Why ask such a question?"
I have already stated previously: if I possess affection and craving, I shall be born again in a future life;
if I am without affection and craving, I shall not be born again.
Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, there is a man who serves a king with all his might; the king, recognizing his merit, should grant him wealth and goods.
Having received these goods, the man would use them extensively for himself—clothing, bedding, food, drink, and various pleasures—for his own enjoyment."
That man argued, saying:
"I have rendered service to the King, yet the King has never bestowed any reward upon me.
Nāgasena asked the King:
"If that person, having received a reward, were instead to say he had never received it—
would his words be acceptable?
The King replied:
"The words of that man are not to be relied upon. Nāgasena said:
"For this reason, I said to the King: 'If I possess craving (*tṛṣṇā*), I shall be born again in a future life; if I am without craving, I shall not be born again in a future life.'"
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
Then the king asked Nāgasena:
"You previously spoke of 'name' and 'body'; what is meant by name, and what is meant by body? Nāgasena replied:
"That which is presently existing is the body; that which is conceived by the mind is the name."
The king asked again:
"For what reason does a person have a name that persists in future lives, while the body itself does not persist in those lives?
Nāgasena replied:
“The human person is constituted by the connection between name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
Just as an egg is formed from the yolk within and the outer shell,
so too is the person inseparable from the connection between name and form.”
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'long'? Nāgasena replied,
"Past events are long, and future events are also long."
"Present phenomena do not endure for long.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Is it certain that there has been such a long duration? Nāgasena replied:
"Sometimes there is duration, and sometimes there is no duration.
The King spoke again:
"What is meant by 'there is duration'?"
"What is meant by 'not having long'? Nāgasena replied:
"Those who have attained the Way and Nirvāṇa do not have long; those who have not yet attained the Way and must undergo further birth and death do have long."
"If a person in this present life delights in giving alms and is filial toward their parents, they shall obtain its blessings in a future life.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Regarding all matters of the past, the future, and those presently occurring—of these three types of matters, what is their fundamental basis?"
Nāgasena said: "Regarding past events, future events, and present events, ignorance (*avidyā*) is their root.

From ignorance arises the soul (*ātman*); from the soul arises the body; from the body arises name (*nāman*); from name arises form (*rūpa*); from form arise the six cognitions: first, visual cognition; second, auditory cognition; third, olfactory cognition; fourth, gustatory cognition; fifth, tactile cognition; and sixth, mental cognition. These are the six cognitions, and these six things all turn outward."
What constitutes the outward-directed?

The eye is directed toward forms, the ear toward sounds, the nose toward odors, the tongue toward tastes, the body toward tactile sensations, and the mind toward sensual desire; these are the six external [objects].

What was formerly called "péi" (overflowing) means "convergence. Péi means knowing suffering and knowing pleasure. From suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving arises acquisition, which in turn gives rise to old age; from old age arises illness; from illness arises death; from death arises weeping; from weeping arises sorrow; and from sorrow arises inner anguish.
All that is combined through these various hardships is collectively termed "human.
Because of this, birth and death for humans have no time of cessation; thus, the original substance of a human being cannot be found.

Nāgasena said: "It is like a person who sows the five grains; from the roots they grow stalks, leaves, and fruit, and later, once the grain has been obtained, he sows again the following year and obtains a great abundance of grain."
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person sows grain, sowing it year after year; would there ever come a time when it ceases to grow?
The king replied:
"Year after year one plants grain; there is never a time when it does not grow.
Nāgasena said: "The birth of human beings is also like this; they are born from one another in succession, and there is no time when this process ceases."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a hen laying an egg and an egg producing a hen; from the egg comes an egg, and from the hen comes a hen.
The birth and death of humans is also like this; there is no time when it ceases."
Nāgasena then drew a wheel on the ground and asked the king,
"Does this wheel have any horns?
The king replied:
"It is perfectly round and has no corners.
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha’s sūtras state that the cycle of human birth and death is like a wheel; they revolve and produce one another in succession without a moment's cessation."

Nāgasena said: "A person, through the eye, external objects, and forms, gives rise to consciousness and thereby perceives; these three things combine. From this combination, suffering and pleasure arise; from suffering and pleasure, affection arises; from affection, craving arises; from craving, the cause of rebirth arises; from the cause of rebirth, birth arises; and from the causes of birth, one performs good and evil deeds; from good and evil deeds, [rebirth] is produced."

When the ear hears a sound, consciousness immediately perceives it; these three factors come together, and from their conjunction arise suffering and pleasure. From suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving arises the cause that leads to existence; from the cause that leads to existence arises birth; and from birth arise good and evil deeds, from which [rebirth] subsequently arises.

When the nose smells an odor, consciousness immediately perceives it; when these three factors come together, suffering and pleasure arise from their conjunction. From suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving arises the cause of existence; from the cause of existence arises birth; and from the cause of birth one performs good and evil deeds, from which rebirth subsequently occurs.

When the mouth obtains a flavor, consciousness immediately perceives it; when these three factors come together, suffering and pleasure arise from that conjunction. From suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving arises the causal condition for rebirth. From the causal condition for rebirth, action arises; from action, good and evil arise; and from good and evil, birth occurs.

When the body attains subtle and smooth sensations, consciousness immediately perceives them; when these three factors come together, suffering and pleasure arise from their conjunction. From suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving arises the cause that leads to existence; from the cause that leads to existence arises birth; and from the cause of birth, one performs good and evil deeds, from which rebirth subsequently occurs.

When the mind has an object of thought, consciousness immediately perceives it; these three factors come together, and from their conjunction, suffering and pleasure arise. From suffering and pleasure, affection arises; from affection, craving arises; from craving, the cause that leads to rebirth arises. From this cause that leads to rebirth, action—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is performed; and from such action, birth subsequently arises.
Nāgasena said: "Human beings are born from one another in succession without end.
The King asked:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"You say that the origin of birth and death for human beings cannot be found."
"What is the meaning of 'unattainable'? Nāgasena replied,
"That which has a beginning shall not be born again."
"If there were a fundamental basis, it would have to pass away again; why then is this considered the basis?
The King said, "That which has no fundamental basis shall not be born again."
"If one sees that which has a beginning, it must have passed away;
is such a beginning not yet severed? Nāgasena replied, "Indeed."
"All shall pass away.
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"In the birth and death of humans, is there anything that comes from the side to augment them?"
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Among the people of the world and the various classes of crawling and wriggling creatures, are there any who increase from the side?
The king replied:
"I do not ask about those people of former lives, nor about the crawling and wriggling creatures; I wish only to ask you about the root of birth and death for human beings. Nāgasena said:
"When trees grow, they take the seed as their root."
The five grains grow, taking the grain itself as their root.
All things in the world each take their own kind as their root of birth; human beings take the six passions and affectionate attachment as their root.

Nāgasena said: "A person has eyes, forms, and consciousness; ears, sounds, and consciousness; a nose, odors, and consciousness; a tongue, tastes, and consciousness; a body, tangibles, and consciousness; and mindfulness, mental objects, and consciousness. From these arise pleasure and pain; from pleasure and pain arises affection; from affection arises craving; and from craving [all things] arise. It is through the combination of all these sufferings that one becomes a person."

The eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, and consciousness give rise to existence; when these are combined, they form a mass. From this mass arise suffering and pleasure; from suffering and pleasure arises affection; from affection arises craving; from craving as a cause arises existence; from existence as a cause arises birth; from birth as a cause arise old age and illness; from illness as a cause arises death; from death as a cause arises sorrow; from sorrow as a cause arises weeping; from weeping as a cause arises inner anguish. Such is the nature of human life.

Nāgasena said: "Without the eye, one does not see forms; one does not perceive or know them. From this lack of perception and knowledge, there is no contact. Where there is no contact, there is no suffering or pleasure. Where there is no suffering or pleasure, affection does not arise. Where there is no affection, craving does not arise. Where there is no craving, there is no becoming. Where there is no becoming, there is no birth or aging. Where there is no birth or aging, there is no sickness or death. Where there is no sickness or death, there is no sorrow or lamentation. Where there is no sorrow or lamentation, there is no inner anguish. When these various sufferings are absent, one attains liberation and the path of Nirvāṇa."

Without ears, there is nothing heard; without a nose, there is nothing smelled; without a mouth, there is nothing tasted; without a body, there is no touch of the subtle or smooth; without consciousness, there is nothing thought; without what is thought, there is no craving; without craving, there is no suffering or pleasure; without suffering or pleasure, there is no affection; without affection, there is no desire; without desire, there is no womb; without a womb, there is no birth; not being born, one does not age; not aging, one does not fall ill; not falling ill, one does not die; not dying, one does not grieve; not grieving, one does not weep; not weeping, there is no inner pain in the heart. Having cast off all sufferings, one attains the Way of Nirvana.
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there anything in the world that arises spontaneously without cause?
Nāgasena replied, "There is nothing that arises spontaneously; all things must have a cause."
Nāgasena then asked the king:
"Was this palace where Your Majesty now sits constructed by human labor,
or did it arise spontaneously?"
The King said:
"Human labor produces it; the timber for the rafters comes from trees, and the mud for the walls comes from the earth. Nāgasena said:
"Human life is also like this: it is through the coming together of the elements (*dhātu*) that one becomes a person.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a spontaneously arising being; all things have their causes."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a potter making vessels: he takes clay and mixes it with water to form mud, which he then fires to produce various kinds of vessels.
That mud cannot become a vessel by itself; it must necessarily depend on human labor and the fire of fuel to become a vessel."
"In this world, there is nothing that arises spontaneously.
Nāgasena said to the king:
"Suppose, for example, there were a lute without strings and without frets, and no one to play it—could it produce sound?"
The king said, "It cannot produce sound by itself. Nāgasena said:
“If a *konghou* lute has strings and frets, and there is someone skilled at playing it, would its sound not emerge?
The King said, “It would have sound.”
Nāgasena said: "In this world, there is nothing that arises spontaneously; all things must have a cause.
Nāgasena then asked the king:
“Suppose one were to drill for fire; if there were no two pieces of wood and no person to do the drilling, would it be possible to obtain fire?
The King replied, “It would not be possible to obtain fire.”
Nāgasena said: "Suppose there were two pieces of wood and someone were to drill them together; would it be possible to produce fire?
The King said:
"Indeed. Fire shall be produced immediately. Nāgasena said:
"There is nothing in the world that produces things spontaneously;
all must have a cause. Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose there were a sun-stirring mirror (ādityapratibimba); if no one held it, and there were neither sun nor sky, could fire be produced?"
Nāgasena said: "Suppose there is a sun-focusing mirror; if a person holds it, and there is both the sky and the sun, would it be possible to obtain fire?
The King said:
"Fire has been obtained.
Nāgasena said: "In this world, there is nothing that produces life spontaneously; everything must have a cause."
Nāgasena asked the king:
"If a person has neither a mirror nor a lamp, and that person wishes to look at themselves, would they be able to see their own form?
The king said:
"It cannot see itself," Nāgasena said.
"Suppose there were a mirror and light, and a person were to look at themselves; would they be able to see their own form?"
The king said, “Indeed. One can see it for oneself.”
Nāgasena said, "In this world, there is nothing that produces living beings spontaneously; all things have causes.
The King said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there truly a person in this world, or is there not?"
Nāgasena said: "In this world, one cannot definitively establish that a person exists.
To whom, then, should one properly apply the designation 'person'?"
The king said:
"Is the life within the body itself the person?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Within this human body, can the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) use the eyes to see forms?
Can it use the ears to hear sounds?
Can it use the nose to smell fragrances?"
Can the tongue perceive tastes?
Can the body perceive tactile sensations?
Can the mind perceive objects of cognition?
The king said, “I can. Nāgasena said:
"Now, as for me and the King, since there are windows on all four sides of this hall, if we wish to look out from whichever window we please, would we be able to see?
The King replied,
"We would be able to see."
Nāgasena said: "Suppose a person’s life-force were within their body; could they freely choose through which orifice to look out?
Could one see forms with the eye?"
Can one see forms with the ears?
Can one see forms with the nose?
Can one see forms with the mouth?
"Can one use the body to see forms?
Can one use the mind to see forms?
The King replied:
"No," said Nāgasena, "even if one's life were at its very end, would one still be able to hear with the ears?"
Can one see with the ear? Can one know fragrances and stenches with the ear?
Can one know tastes with the ear?
“Can one perceive smoothness with the ear?
Can one have thoughts with the ear?
Nāgasena replied:
"Suppose one's life were dependent upon the nose; would one still be able to know fragrances and stenches with the nose?
Would one be able to hear sounds with the nose?
Would one be able to know tastes with the nose?"
"Can the nose perceive subtle and smooth sensations? Can the nose have thoughts?
Nāgasena replied:
"Even if one's life were at the point of the mouth, could one perceive flavors with the mouth?
Could one see anything with the mouth?
Could one hear sounds with the mouth?"
Can one perceive fragrant or foul odors with the mouth?
Can one know tactile sensations with the mouth?
Can one have thoughts with the mouth?
Nāgasena said: "Suppose life were within the body; could one know smoothness and roughness with the body?
Could one see anything with the body?"
Can one hear sounds with the body?
Can one perceive odors with the body?
Can one perceive tastes with the body?
"Can the body think by means of what it possesses?
Nāgasena replied, "Suppose life were to reside in consciousness; could consciousness then think by means of what it possesses?"
Can one use consciousness to hear sounds?
Can one use consciousness to know fragrances and odors?
Can one use consciousness to know tastes?
"Can one perceive smoothness through consciousness?
The King replied,
"One cannot perceive it."
Nāgasena said: "What Your Majesty has said is inconsistent from beginning to end. Nāgasena continued:
"If I were sitting with the King upon the palace terrace, and all four windows were completely broken open, would the view not be vast and far-reaching?
The King said, "Indeed it would."
"Is it far-reaching? Nāgasena said:
"Suppose life were within the body; if one were to pluck out the eyes and remove them, would its vision still be far-reaching?"
If one were to enlarge the ears, would their hearing then be able to reach further?
If one were to enlarge the nose, would they then be able to smell fragrances from further away?
If one were to enlarge the mouth, would they then be able to perceive more flavors?
“If one were to flay the skin from his body, would you know its subtle smoothness as being much?
Would your resolve to depart be even greater? The King said:
"No," said Nāgasena, "the King's words, too, are inconsistent from beginning to end."
Nāgasena asked the king: "Suppose a treasurer were brought before you and stood in your presence; would you be aware that he was standing there?
The king replied:
"Knowledge comes first.
Nāgasena said: "When a treasurer enters the royal palace, do you know whether he has entered the room or not?"
The King said,
"I know he has entered the room. Nāgasena said:
"Suppose that human life were present within the body, and a person held a flavor in their mouth; they would be able to know whether it was sweet, sour, bitter, salty, pungent, or astringent.
The King said, "I know this."
Nāgasena said: "What Your Majesty has said is inconsistent from beginning to end. Nāgasena continued:

"Suppose a person were to pour fine wine into a large vessel, quickly stop one person's mouth, and turn them upside down into the wine to have them taste it; would that person know the flavor of the wine?"
The king said, "That man does not know. Nāgasena said:
"Why is it that he does not know the taste?
The king replied,
"Because it has not yet entered the mouth and reached the tongue, he does not know the taste."
Nāgasena said, "What Your Majesty has said is inconsistent from beginning to end. The King said:
"I am foolish; my wisdom has not yet reached the depth of this difficulty. I pray that you will explain it to me. Nāgasena said:
"When a person sees a form with the eye, the spirit (ātman) moves; as the spirit moves, suffering and pleasure arise."

The mind unites with the ears, nose, mouth, and body; the mind unites with them all alike. Because the spirit moves when the mind has something to contemplate, suffering and pleasure arise from that movement of the spirit. From suffering and pleasure, intention arises; from this arising intention, thoughts develop and mutually reinforce one another, yet they remain devoid of any permanent master.
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person's eye exists, is the eye born together with the spirit?
Nāgasena replied, "Yes."
"They arise simultaneously.
The King asked again:
"Does the eye arise before?"
"Does the spirit arise before the body?
Nāgasena replied, "The eye arises first; the spirit arises later."
The King said: "The Eye-Speech Deity said:
'In whatever place of birth I am to be reborn, you shall follow me and be reborn there.'"
The two deities spoke to one another: "O deity,
regarding the place where you shall be born, I shall follow behind you and be born there as well."
“Did those two speak with one another? Nāgasena replied,
“The two did not speak with each other.”
The King said, "If you say they were born at the same time, for what reason do they not speak to one another?
Nāgasena replied:
"There are four things that do not speak to one another. Nāgasena said:
"What are these four?"
"First is the downward path, second is the approach to the gate, third is the track of travel, and fourth is the numbering.
These four matters do not speak to one another.
The King asked again:
"What is meant by 'those who go downward'?
Nāgasena replied to the king:
"When it rains upon a high mountain, how does that water flow along with the current?"
The King said, "Go down. Nāgasena replied:
Later, when it rained again, [the king asked], "How will that water flow?
The king replied,
"It shall flow along the same course as the previous stream."
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Would the preceding water say to the succeeding water,
'You should follow me and come after'?"
Then the later water says to the earlier water:
"I shall flow along following your course.
Do the earlier and later waters speak to one another in this way?
The king said, "The currents of water each flow on their own; those before and those behind do not speak to one another. Nāgasena said:
"The eye is also like water.
The eye does not speak to the spirit, saying:
'You should follow after me and be born.'"
The deity likewise does not speak to the eye, saying:
"I shall follow behind you in rebirth.
The eye and the deity do not converse with one another; this is called the lower course.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The King asked again:
"What is meant by 'tending toward the gate'?"
Nāgasena said: "Suppose there is a great city with only one gate, and within it there is a person who wishes to go out; by which direction should he proceed?
The King said:
"One must exit through the gate," Nāgasena said.
"If another person later wishes to exit, by which direction should they go out?"
The king said, "Therefore,
it must have been the first person who went out through the gate. Nāgasena said:
“O King! Does the person who goes out first say to the person behind:
‘You should follow after me’?”
Would the person behind say to the person in front:
"I shall follow you out through whichever gate you depart from"?
Would the two of them not speak to one another in such a manner?
The King said,
"The former person and the latter person do not speak with one another. Nāgasena said:
"The eye is also like a gate.
The eye does not say to the spirit:
'You should be born following after me.'"
The spirit likewise does not say to the eye:
"I shall now be born following after you.
The eye and the spirit do not speak to one another; this is what is meant by "facing the gate."
"The same applies to the ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'those who follow the tracks'?"
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When a preceding carriage has passed, there is a track; from where should a subsequent carriage follow?
The king said:
"The carriage behind should follow the ruts made by the carriage in front.
Nāgasena said: "Does the front wheel ever speak to the rear wheel, saying:"
"You should follow my position from behind.
Would the rear wheel ever say to the front wheel,
"I shall travel following your position"?
"Would you two have spoken to one another?
The king replied,
"We did not speak to each other at all."
Nāgasena said: "A person is also like this.
The eye does not speak to the spirit:”
"Wherever I am born, you should follow me into birth.
Yet the spirit does not say to the eye:
"I shall be born after you."
Nāgasena said: "The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind do not converse with one another.
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is reckoning? Nāgasena replied, "Reckoning means calculation;
writing, commentaries, and learning constitute reckoning."

The ears, eyes, nose, mouth, body, and consciousness gradually learn through practice and combine; it is these six factors that constitute having knowledge, for knowledge does not arise from any single factor alone.
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person's eye first arises, does it arise together with suffering and pleasure?
Nāgasena replied, "The eye arises together with suffering and pleasure; all faculties arise from the conjunction [of conditions]."
The King spoke again:
"What is meant by 'conjunction'? Nāgasena replied:
"The meeting of two things constitutes conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Conjunction is, for example, like two rams butting heads; this is conjunction.
One ram is like the eye, and the other ram is like visible form (*rūpa*); their meeting constitutes the name 'collision' (*pratihata*)."
It is like one hand acting as the eye and the other hand acting as the form; when the two hands join together, they constitute contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
It is like two stones: one stone acts as the eye and the other stone acts as the form; when the two stones join together, they constitute contact.
The ears, eyes, nose, body, and spirit all combine together to form the *pài*.
It is like two stones: one stone is like the spirit and the other stone is like the will; when the two stones combine, they form the *pài*.
"When the spirit and the mind are thus united, this is called 'overflowing' (pài).
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"What kind of things do you find pleasant? Nāgasena replied:
"One personally experiences it as pleasure. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a person who serves a king; if that person is virtuous and good, the king bestows wealth and goods upon him."
Having obtained it, that person uses it for his own pleasure, doing whatever he desires.
He thinks to himself:
"I served the king and received rewards; now I have attained such joy and happiness."
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person whose mind thinks good thoughts, whose speech utters good words, and whose body performs good deeds.
By practicing goodness in this way, after death one is reborn in the heavens."
That person, enjoying themselves to their heart's content in the heavens, thinks to themselves:

"While I was in the world, my mind thought of what is good, my speech spoke of what is good, and my body performed what is good; therefore, I have come to be born in this place and attained such happiness and great joy."
"This is awakening," the King said. "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"What is an awakened one? Nāgasena replied:
"From knowledge comes awakening.

It is like a king who has a treasurer enter the treasury chamber and look within; he knows for himself how much money, gold, silver, pearls, and jade there are, and he knows all the various colors of silks and incenses, knowing exactly where each is placed."
"This is what constitutes awakening.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person has a thought, what kind of thing is it?
Nāgasena replied:
"When a person has a certain thought, they consequently perform a certain action.
It is like a person who mixes a poisonous drug and drinks it themselves, and furthermore administers it to others; thus they suffer their own body and likewise cause the bodies of others to suffer."
Nāgasena said: "For example, if a person commits evil, they shall enter hell after death; likewise, all those whom they have taught shall also enter hell."
"An evil person has such thoughts, deeds, and speech.
The King said: "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that moves within? Nāgasena replied:
"When the will and mindfulness stir within," the King asked,
"What is it like when they move and act?"

Nāgasena said: "Suppose, for example, there were copper pans or copper cauldrons, and someone were to go and heat them; those vessels would make a sound, and even after they are lifted up, a lingering resonance remains."
"Yet for the practitioner, it is thus: the movement of the will and the cause of thought constitute 'action' (saṃskāra). Nāgasena said:
"At the time of burning, there is movement; when there is residual sound, that is 'action'."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“Can you distinguish that which unites and grasps?
Is this union, is this wisdom, is this mindfulness, is this mind, or is this movement?
Nāgasena replied:
"Even if they are combined, they can no longer be distinguished. Nāgasena said:
"Suppose Your Majesty were to have a cook prepare a fine soup; within it there would be water, meat, scallions and garlic, ginger, salt and fermented soybeans, and glutinous rice."
The king commanded his kitchen staff, saying:

"Of the fine soup you have prepared, first bring me the taste of the water from within it; next, bring me the taste of the leeks; next, bring me the taste of the ginger; next, bring me the taste of the salt and fermented soybeans; and next, bring me the taste of the glutinous rice."
“When the soup has been prepared, would a person be able to take out each individual flavor of the soup and give it to the King?
The King replied,
“Once the soup is blended into a single mixture, one cannot distinguish each flavor individually.”
Nāgasena said: "All things are likewise;
when combined into a unity, they cannot be distinguished. How then can one say, 'This is suffering or pleasure,' 'This is wisdom,' 'This is motion,' or 'This is mindfulness'?"
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"If a person were to look at salt with their eyes, would they be able to distinguish its taste?
Nāgasena replied,
"Does Your Majesty understand it in this way?"
"Can the eye perceive the taste of salt by looking at it?
The King said,
"Does the eye not know the taste of salt?"
Nāgasena said: "A person, by means of the tongue, can perceive the taste of salt, but cannot perceive the taste of salt with the eyes.
The king spoke again:
"Is it that people know flavors with the tongue? Nāgasena replied,
"All people distinguish and know flavors with the tongue."
The King asked,
"Must all the flavors of salt be distinguished by means of the tongue? Nāgasena replied:
"Indeed. All salt flavors must be distinguished by the tongue alone.
The King questioned Nāgasena again, saying:
"If salt is carried by a cart or on an ox-yoke, are the cart and the ox able to distinguish the taste of the salt?
Nāgasena replied,
"The cart and the ox cannot distinguish the taste of the salt."
The King asked Nāgasena,
"Can the taste of salt be weighed?
Nāgasena replied:
"The King's wisdom is indeed such that he can weigh the taste of salt.
The King asked Nāgasena, "The taste of salt cannot be weighed; it is only its weight that can be weighed."
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“Is it that the five consciousnesses within the body of an ordinary person perform various tasks,
or do they perform a single task and thereby become five consciousnesses? Nāgasena replied:
"It is accomplished through the convergence of many conditions, not by a single condition alone.
For example, on a single field, when the five grains are about to grow, each grows according to its own nature."
“Regarding the category of movement, the five factors within the human body are all produced by their respective conditions.
The King said: “Excellent, excellent!”
The King asked Nāgasena again:

"In this world, people are all complete with hair, beard, skin, face, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, four limbs, hands, and feet; for what reason are there some whose lifespans are long and others whose lifespans are short? Why are there those who are sickly and those who have little illness? Why are there the poor and the wealthy, the noble and the lowly, the great men and the small men, the handsome and the ugly, those who are trusted by others and those who are doubted by others, and those who are wise and filial and those who are foolish?"
"Why are they not the same? Nāgasena replied:
"For example, among the fruits of various trees, some are sour and not sweet; among them, some are bitter, some are pungent, some are sweet, and some are intensely sour."
Nāgasena asked the king, "All these are trees; why are they not the same? The king said:
"The reason they differ is that their individual dispositions (*karman*) are each distinct.
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for human beings;

what the mind conceives of differs from one to another, and it is for this reason that people in the world are not alike. Among them, some have short lives and some have long lives; some have many ailments and some have few ailments; some are wealthy and some are poor; some are noble and some are lowly; some are great persons and some are small persons; some are handsome and some are ugly; some are eloquent and some are not eloquent; some are wise and some are foolish."
Nāgasena said: "Therefore, that which the Buddha spoke is true: according to the good or evil one has done, one shall receive the fruit thereof for oneself.

Among those there are some who are noble and wealthy, and among them some who are poor; all of these are due to the good or evil they performed in their previous lives, each receiving their lot according to their own merit."
The king said, "Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"If a person wishes to perform a good deed, should they do it beforehand,
or should they do it afterwards? Nāgasena replied:
"One should act while standing at the front;
acting from behind cannot benefit others, whereas acting while standing at the front is beneficial to others.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When the king is thirsty and wishes to drink, if he were to have men dig a well in the ground, would it be able to quench the king's thirst?
The king replied, "It would not quench his thirst; one must dig the well beforehand."
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for people.
Those whom a person dwells with should always be placed before him; to place them behind is of no benefit."
Nāgasena asked the king, "When you are hungry,
do you have someone plow the fields, manure the soil, and sow grain? Is it for the sake of a meal that you perform these tasks,
or should there be a store of provisions in advance?"
The king said: “No.
One must first have provisions stored.”
Nāgasena said, "It is the same for a person:
one should first perform wholesome deeds; to perform wholesome deeds only when in an emergency is of no benefit to oneself.
Nāgasena then asked the king:
“Suppose, for example, a king has an enemy and the time for battle approaches; can the king employ others to train his horses and elephants, and instruct his men in the arts of warfare?”
The king said: "No.
One must have stores and provisions prepared in advance; only then can one engage in battle when the time comes."
"To temporarily train horses, elephants, or humans is of no benefit.
Nāgasena said: "The Buddhist scriptures state:"
"A person should first consider practicing virtue for themselves; it is of no benefit to practice virtue only afterwards.
Nāgasena said, "Your Majesty, do not abandon the Great Way to follow a deviant path."
Foolish people who act ineffectually, abandoning the good to commit evil, will later sit in weeping; it will be of no benefit.
When a family abandons the loyal and upright for the unrighteous, they will only feel regret at the time of death.
The king said, “Excellent, excellent!
The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"You śramaṇas have said:
'The fire of the world is not as hot as the fire in the hells.
Yet you have also said:"
If one takes a small stone and places it within the fires of this world, it will not be consumed even by evening.
You all, however, say that if one takes an extremely large stone and places it within the fires of niraya, it is immediately consumed and exhausted.
For this reason, I do not believe it.
You all further say:
"If a person commits evil, they shall die and dwell in the hells for many tens of millions of years; that person does not perish even through death."
"Therefore, I again do not believe these words.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Have you ever heard of or seen female pythons, female sea serpents, female turtles, or female crabs conceiving offspring in the water and feeding on sand and stones?"
The king said, "Indeed.
All of them take this as their food."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Would sand and gravel in the stomach ever be digested?
The king replied:
"Yes, they are all digested," Nāgasena said.
"Will the child conceived within her womb ever be digested?
The King replied,
"It will not be digested."
Nāgasena asked, "For what reason does it not digest?
The King replied:
Nagasena said: "The person whose fortune is naturally such that it does not diminish is like this;
those in the hells are also like this."
"As for those who have not been digested and die after tens of millions of years, it is because the transgressions committed by that person are not yet exhausted;
therefore, they do not die from digestion. Nāgasena asked the king:
"When a female lion, a female tiger, a female dog, or a female cat conceives offspring, since they all eat meat and devour bones, when these enter their bellies, are they not digested?"
The king said, "They have all been consumed. Nāgasena asked the king:
“Will the child in her womb ever pass away?
The king replied,
“It will not pass away.”
Nāgasena asked, "For what reason does it not digest?
The King replied:
"Because they alone enjoy the fruits of their merit, it does not diminish. Nāgasena said:
"Those in the hells (niraya) are also like this."

"As for those who do not die for tens of millions of years without their [karmic] retribution being exhausted, it is because the transgressions and evils committed by those in the *niraya* have not yet been resolved;
therefore, they do not die from exhaustion. Nāgasena asked the King:
"Do female cows, female horses, female donkeys, female elk, and female deer that are pregnant all eat grass and fodder for their meals?"
The king said, "Indeed.
All of them take this as their food."
Nāgasena asked: "Would that straw be digested and consumed within the belly?
The King said:
"Everything has been digested and exhausted," Nāgasena said.
"Would the fetus within her womb also be digested and exhausted?"
The king said, "It has not been completely consumed. Nāgasena said:
"Why does it not exhaust?
The king replied,
"It is solely because of the natural course of my karmic fortune that it does not exhaust."
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for those in the hells; because their transgressions have not yet been exhausted, they do not die.
Nāgasena then asked the king:
"The lady and the daughters of wealthy householders eat food that is all delicious and eat to their heart's content.
Does it digest peacefully within their bellies?
The King said:
"All are digested," he said. Nāgasena asked the king,
"If one carries a child in the womb, will it also be digested?"
The king said, "It cannot be digested. Nāgasena said:
"Why does it not digest?
The king replied,
"It is because of the singular power of my sovereign fortune that it does not digest."
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for those in the hells.
The reason they do not die for thousands of years without their bodies decaying is because of the evil deeds committed in previous lives; because these have not yet been exhausted, they do not die."
Nāgasena said: "A person grows old while in the hells and dies only when that duration has fully elapsed.
The King asked:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Your various śramaṇas say:..."
"The entire earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; and wind rests upon space.
I do not believe this.
Then Nāgasena stepped forward, took up some water from the king's vessel, picked it up with three fingers, and asked the king: "Is this so?"
“Is this water supported by wind? The king replied,
“Indeed it is.”
"It is sustained by wind. Nāgasena said,
"Wind sustaining water is also like this."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the path to Nirvāṇa all pass away, so that nothing remains?
Nāgasena replied, "In the path to Nirvāṇa, nothing remains."
Nāgasena said: "The foolish person comes directly to seek the love for the internal and external body; because of this, they are unable to attain liberation from old age, sickness, and death."

Nāgasena said: "The wise practitioner of the Path does not cling to the body internally or externally. When one has no endearment or affection (*sneha*), there is no craving (*rāga*). One who has no craving has no womb of rebirth (*garbha*). One who has no womb of rebirth is neither born nor grows old; being neither born nor growing old, they do not fall ill nor die. Being free from illness, they have no sorrow or weeping. Being free from sorrow and weeping, they have no inner mental anguish, and thus they attain the Way of Nirvāṇa."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Can all those who practice the Path attain the Way of Nirvana?
Nāgasena replied,
"They cannot all attain the Way of Nirvana."

Those who are correctly oriented toward the wholesome path learn to know what is right; they practice that which ought to be practiced and distance themselves from that which ought not to be practiced;
they contemplate that which ought to be contemplated and abandon that which ought not to be contemplated.
"A person who is thus attains the path of Nirvana.
The King said: "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If a person has not attained the path of Nirvāṇa, can they know whether the path of Nirvāṇa is blissful?
Nāgasena replied:
"But it is so. Although one has not yet attained the path to Nirvana, by knowing the path to Nirvana, one finds joy.
The King said:
"If a person has not yet attained the path of Nirvāṇa, how can they know what it is to be joyful?
Nāgasena asked the king,
"When a person has never had their hands or feet cut off, which would be the place of greatest pain?"
The King said:
"Although a person has never before had their hands or feet cut off, they still know what pain is. Nāgasena said:
"What is the use of knowing that it is pain?
The king said, "When that person has his hands and feet cut off, he cries out; it is by this that one knows it is pain."
Nāgasena said: "It is the same with human beings.
Those who have previously attained the path to Nirvāṇa speak to one another of how delightful the path to Nirvāṇa is; for this reason, people believe it."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Nagasena, have you ever seen the Buddha?
Nagasena replied, "I have never seen him."
The King asked,
"Nāgasena, have you teachers ever seen the Buddha?
Nāgasena replied:
“The various masters have also not seen the Buddha.
“If Nāgasena and the various masters have not seen the Buddha, it must be that the Buddha does not exist at all.”
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Does Your Majesty see the place where five hundred streams converge?
The king replied:
"I do not see it," [the King] replied. Nāgasena said:
"Did your father and grandfather both see this water?"
The King said, "I see none of them. Nāgasena said:

"Your Majesty, neither your father nor your grandfather ever saw this place where these five hundred waters converge. Is it therefore certain that no such place where these five hundred waters gather exists anywhere in the world?"
The King said,
"Although neither I, nor my father, nor my grandfather has ever seen this water,
it truly exists. Nāgasena said:
"Although my teachers have not seen the Buddha, in truth there is a Buddha.
The King said: "Excellent!"

*The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena*, Lower Volume.
