The king asked again, "Is there anyone superior to the Buddha? Nāgasena replied, "Indeed, there is no one superior to the Buddha.
The king asked once more:
"How do you know that there is no Buddha superior to him?
Nāgasena asked the king, saying:
"Suppose a person has never entered the great ocean; would he know whether the waters of the ocean are vast or not?"
There are five rivers; into each river flow five hundred small tributaries. The first is named Gaṅgā, the second Sindhū, the third Sītā, the fourth Vakṣu, and the fifth Śatadru.
"Those five rivers flow into the sea day and night, yet the seawater neither increases nor decreases.
Nāgasena said: "Does Your Majesty not know this?"
The King said, “I truly know. Nāgasena said:
"Because those who have attained the Way discourse together on the Way, and none can surpass the Buddha, for this reason I believe him.
The King said: "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"How do you know that there is no one who can surpass the Buddha?
Nāgasena asked the King:
"Who was the scribe who composed it?
The king replied,
"The scribe who composed it was named Qi."
Nāgasena said: "Your Majesty, have you ever seen a reflection?
The King replied:
“Citra has been dead for a very long time; I have never seen him. Nāgasena said:
“Your Majesty has never seen Citra; how then do you know that Citra was the master calligrapher?”
The King said:
"By means of ancient scripts and characters, people transmit teachings and inform one another; for this reason, I know that it is called 'substance' (dharma). Nāgasena said:
"For this reason, when we see the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts, it is no different from seeing the Buddha himself.

The Dharma taught by the Buddha in these sūtras is profoundly deep and most excellent; once people have come to know the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts, they in turn teach one another. For this reason, I know that there is none who can surpass the Buddha."
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"I have seen that the Buddha’s scriptures and the Way can be practiced for a long time. Nāgasena said:
“The teachings, prohibitions, sutras, and precepts bestowed by the Buddha are most excellent; we shall uphold and practice them until old age. The King said, “Excellent!”
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"After a person has died, does the body not follow them into birth in a future life?
Nāgasena replied:
"Once a person has died, they receive a new body; therefore, the old body does not follow. Nāgasena said:
"It is like a lamp where the wick is successively ignited; thus the wick continues to exist while a new wick is lit."
"The human body is like this: when the current body does not practice [the Way], one receives a new body.
Nāgasena asked the king, "When you were young, did you follow a teacher to learn writing and read the scriptures?"
The King said, “Indeed.
I shall continue to keep it in mind.”
Nāgasena asked the king:
"The teacher from whom Your Majesty received the scriptures—does that teacher still know those original scriptures?
Does he still possess those original scriptures?"
The king said:
"No, Master. You yourself merely know the original scripture."
Nāgasena said: "The human body is like this: it is cast off and a new body is received.
The King said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again,
"Is it certain that you possess wisdom?"
Nāgasena said: "There is no such thing as knowledge. Nāgasena said:
“Suppose, for example, a person steals another’s fruits or melons; would that thief not be guilty?
The King said, “He would be guilty.”
Nāgasena said: "When a plant is first sown, there is no fruit or gourd upon it; on what grounds, then, would a thief be guilty?
The King asked:
"If one does not plant the seed, by what cause could there be fruit?
Therefore, the thief's conduct is without justification. Nāgasena said:
"Human beings are also like this:
by performing good or evil deeds in this life, they are born in a future life and receive a new body.
The King said:
“Because of this, people perform good and evil deeds with their bodies; where do these new good and evil reside?
Nāgasena replied:
“Whatever a person does, their good and evil follow them, just as a shadow follows the body.”
When a person dies, only their body perishes, but not their conduct.
It is like writing by fire at night: when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain; when the fire returns, they are once again made manifest.
"What one does in this life will be realized accordingly in the next life; one receives its fruit in such a manner.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King said:
"Nāgasena, are you able to distinguish and point out exactly where good and evil reside?
Nāgasena replied:
"One cannot know where good and evil reside.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"When a tree has not yet borne fruit, can one distinguish and point out, saying that there is no fruit among its branches?"
"Would it not be better to know this beforehand?
The king replied,
"It cannot be known."
Nāgasena said, "A person who has not yet attained the Way cannot know in advance where good and evil reside.
The King said:
"Excellent! The king asked again:
"When a person is to be born in a future life, can they know it for themselves?"
Nāgasena said, "Those who are to be born know it themselves.
The King asked:
"What is the use of knowing this?
Nāgasena replied, "Suppose a farmer plows and sows his fields; when the rains come at the proper season, can that man know for certain in advance whether he will obtain grain or not?"
The king said, “Indeed;
one still knows that one shall obtain much grain.”
Nāgasena said: "It is the same for a person.
When a person is to be born in a future life, they know it in advance."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there truly Nirvana? Nāgasena replied,
"There truly is."
The king said, "Nāgasena,
could you perhaps point out to me where the Buddha is? Nāgasena replied:
"One cannot point out that the Buddha is at a certain place.
Since the Buddha has departed through parinirvāṇa, it is impossible to point out or show his location. Nāgasena said:
“Suppose, for example, a person were to light a great fire and then immediately extinguish it; would it be possible to point out where the flame is, or know the location of its light?
The King replied, “Its location cannot be known.”
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa; his whereabouts can no longer be known.
The king said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does a śramaṇa love his own body?"
Nāgasena said, "The śramaṇa does not love his own body.
The king said:

"If a śramaṇa does not love his own body, for what reason would he take care of himself when lying down, seeking comfort; or seek warm, soft food and drink, seeking delicacy; or carefully protect and observe himself? For what reason?"
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Have you ever entered into the midst of battle?
The king replied:
"Yes. I once entered into the midst of battle," Nāgasena replied.
“Have you ever been struck by the edge of a sword or by an arrow in battle?
The King replied,
“I have indeed been struck by the edge of a sword on several occasions.”
Nāgasena asked the king,
"What is it like when one has wounds from sword blades, spears,
or arrows? The king replied:
"I have wrapped my ear with medicinal ointment and cotton wool.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Is it because you love the sore that you wrap it with medicinal ointment and cotton wool?"
The king said,
"Do I not love my wound?
Nāgasena replied:
"If you do not love the ulcer at all, why do you apply medicinal ointment and wrap it with cotton wool to protect it?
The king replied, "I wish only for the illness to be healed; I do not love the ulcer."
Nāgasena said: "The śramaṇa is also like this. He does not cherish his own body;

although he eats and drinks, his mind finds no pleasure in it. He does not seek to make it beautiful, nor to make it attractive, nor to improve its complexion; he merely desires to sustain the physical body so as to practice the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha."
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"A person has nine apertures, which are like nine spear-wounds; all these orifices are foul-smelling and impure.
The king said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the Buddha truly possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, with a body entirely golden in color and surrounded by a halo of light?"
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha truly possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; they are all golden in color and accompanied by halos.
The King said:
“Did the parents of the Buddha also possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, with bodies entirely golden and radiant with light?
Nāgasena replied, “The parents of the Buddha did not have these marks.”
The king said,
"If my parents did not possess these marks, the Buddha likewise would not possess these marks.
The king spoke again:
"A child takes after its kind.
Since the parents do not possess these marks, the Buddha certainly does not possess them. Nāgasena said:
"Although the Buddha’s parents did not possess these thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, nor a golden-colored body, the Buddha certainly possesses these marks.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Have you ever seen a lotus flower?"
The king said, "I have seen it. Nāgasena said:
"This lotus grows from the earth and matures within the mud and water; its color is most fragrant and beautiful. Does it bear any resemblance to the color of the mud and water?
The King replied, "It does not resemble the color of the earth, mud, or water."
Nāgasena said: "Although the Buddha’s parents did not possess these marks, the Buddha truly possesses them.
The Buddha was born into the world and grew up in the world, yet he does not conform to worldly affairs."
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is it true that the Buddha, just like the seventh heavenly king Brahmā, does not engage in sexual intercourse with women?
Nāgasena replied, "It is so."
"He has thoroughly distanced himself from women; he is pure and free from blemish.
The King said, "If the Buddha were to act as the Seventh Heavenly King does, the Buddha would be a disciple of the Seventh Heavenly King Brahmā."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Does the king of the seventh heaven possess mindfulness or not?
The king replied:
"Does the Brahmā, the Seventh Heavenly King,
possess mindfulness? Nāgasena replied,
"For this reason, the Brahmā, the Seventh Heavenly King, and all the higher deities are disciples of the Buddha."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"What kind of sound is the cry of a bird?
The king replied:
"The sound of the birds' calls is like the cry of geese. Nāgasena said:
"Are these birds the disciples of the geese, or are they of a different species?"
"The Buddha is likewise; he is not a disciple of the seventh heavenly king, Brahmā.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again,
"Has the Buddha indeed studied, known, and practiced all the sūtras and precepts?
Nāgasena replied:
“The Buddha has learned, understood, and practiced all the sutras and precepts.
The King asked,
“From what teacher did the Buddha receive the sutras and precepts?”
Nāgasena said: "The Buddha had no teacher.
When the Buddha attained the Way, he fully understood all the teachings and paths by himself."
"The Buddha is not like his disciples who learn what the Buddha has taught; all the disciples shall practice and uphold it until they reach old age.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person's parents die, they weep with grief and tears flow.
When a person hears the Buddha’s sutras, they likewise weep with grief and tears flow."
"When both shed tears, is there any difference between them?
Nāgasena replied, "When people weep for their parents, it is because they are moved by remembrance, affection, gratitude, longing, sorrow, and suffering."
Those who grieve in this manner grieve out of ignorance.

As for those who shed tears upon hearing the Buddha’s sutras and the Way, they all possess a heart of compassion; they contemplate the toil and suffering of the world, and for this reason their tears flow. The merit they obtain is exceedingly great.
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"What is the difference between one who has attained liberation and one who has not?

Nāgasena replied, "A person who has not attained liberation possesses a mind of craving; a person who has attained liberation possesses no mind of craving, desiring only to seek food and drink to sustain their life."
The king said,
"I see that people in the world all desire physical comfort and seek fine food without ever being satisfied. Nāgasena said:
"Those who have not yet attained liberation eat and drink for the sake of honor, pleasure, and enjoyment.
Those who have attained liberation, though they eat and drink, do not regard it as pleasure nor as sweetness; they do so merely to sustain their lives."
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"When people have something to do, do they think of things from long ago?
Nāgasena replied,
"When people are in distress, they all think of things from long ago."
The King asked:
"By what means do you keep it in mind?
Is it by means of mental application (manasikāra)?"
"Is it by means of moment-to-moment [thoughts]? Nāgasena asked the king,
"Have you ever learned something and later recalled it?"
The king said, “Indeed.
There was something I once learned and knew, which I have since suddenly forgotten.”
Nāgasena said: "Was it that Your Majesty did not forget at that time, yet now you have forgotten?
The King replied:
"I was thinking falsely at that time," [the king said].
Nāgasena replied, "It can be explained;
Your Majesty, you do possess elephants."
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person performs an action, is it all through mindfulness? Is it that what has just begun to be done and what is currently being done are both known through mindfulness?"
Nāgasena said, “That which has already passed is known through mindfulness; that which is presently occurring is also known through mindfulness.
The King said:
"Such a person thinks only of past matters and cannot think of new ones again.
Nāgasena said: "Even if there were something to be done regarding a new matter that could not be thought of, it would be just like this."
The King asked,
"Is it a waste for a person who has newly learned writing and crafts?
Nāgasena replied:

"Because those who have newly begun to study calligraphy and painting possess mindfulness, and because I cause my disciples who study them to possess understanding, they therefore possess mindfulness.
The King said: "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"By how many factors does a person give rise to a thought?
Nāgasena replied:

“Ordinary people generally give rise to mindfulness through sixteen matters. First, they give rise to mindfulness regarding what was done long ago; second, they give rise to mindfulness regarding what has newly occurred; third, they give rise to mindfulness regarding significant events; fourth, they give rise to mindfulness by reflecting on the wholesome; fifth, they give rise to mindfulness regarding previously experienced suffering; sixth, they give rise to mindfulness through self-reflection; seventh, they give rise to mindfulness regarding various past actions; eighth, they give rise to mindfulness when others teach them; ninth, they give rise to mindfulness through images; tenth, they give rise to mindfulness regarding things previously forgotten; eleventh, they give rise to mindfulness due to recognition; twelfth, they give rise to mindfulness through calculation; thirteenth, they give rise to mindfulness regarding debts; fourteenth, they give rise to mindfulness with single-minded focus; fifteenth, they give rise to mindfulness while reading books; sixteenth, they give rise to mindfulness upon seeing again something that was previously entrusted to them. These are the sixteen matters through which mindfulness arises.”
1. The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'long-term mindfulness'? Nāgasena replied:
“The Buddha’s disciple Ānanda has a female disciple, the laywoman (upāsikā) Ghoṣadattā, who recollects events from a hundred million past lives.
Furthermore, other practitioners are all able to recollect matters of the past.”
"Just as Ānanda has many younger sisters, he thinks of them and thereby gives rise to thoughts.
Second, the king asked again:
"What is it that constitutes the thoughts newly arising in one who is learning?"
Nāgasena replied:
"It is like a person who once learned and mastered calculation, but later forgot it; upon seeing someone else calculating, he then brings that knowledge back to mind.
Third, the King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'giving rise to thoughts regarding matters of great importance'? Nāgasena replied:

"It is like a crown prince who, upon being established as king, reflects to himself that he has become a king and possesses noble rank; this is what is meant by giving rise to thoughts regarding matters of great importance."
4. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that gives rise to wholesome thoughts?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is, for example, like a person who has been invited by someone else; when that person encounters a guest treated with the utmost kindness, they think to themselves:
'In the past, I was invited by such-and-such a person, who treated me with great kindness.'"
"This is what is meant by 'contemplating the good gives rise to mindfulness.
Fifth, the King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'the renewed arising of suffering gives rise to mindfulness'?"
Nāgasena said: "It is like a person who has previously been beaten and imprisoned by others; this gives rise to the thought of renewed suffering.
6. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'giving rise to mindfulness through self-reflection'?
Nāgasena replied:
"For example, having previously seen one's family, kinsmen, or even animals, this is what is meant by giving rise to mindfulness through self-reflection."
7. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is that which has been performed in the past and gives rise to recollection?
Nāgasena replied:
“Suppose, for example, a person names all things according to their categories—color, fragrance, odor, sweetness, or bitterness—and thinks upon these words and objects;
this is what is meant by ‘mixed thoughts. 8. The King asked Nāgasena again:
“What is it that causes people to give rise to thoughts?”
Nāgasena said: "People naturally delight in forgetting; some among them may possess [the faculty], while others forget. It is for the sake of teaching people to give rise to mindfulness.
9. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'recollection arising from resemblance'? Nāgasena replied:
"Humans, oxen, and horses each have their own respective resemblances; this is what is meant by recollection arising from resemblance."
10. The king asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that one has forgotten yet brings back to mind?
Nāgasena replied:

“It is, for example, like a person who has suddenly forgotten something; by reflecting upon it repeatedly and alone, they recover it—this is what is meant by ‘the arising of a thought from that which was previously forgotten.
11. The King asked Nāgasena again:
“What is the cause for the arising of a thought through consciousness?”
Nāgasena said: "One who studies writing can seek out its characters; this is what is meant by 'thought arises conditioned by consciousness.
12. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'generating thoughts through calculation'? Nāgasena replied:
"It is like when people deliberate together, achieving full understanding and clarifying their strategies; this is what is meant by generating thoughts through calculation."
13. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by 'one who gives rise to thoughts while being in debt'?
Nāgasena replied:
"It is like a debt that must be repaid when the drum is struck; this is what is meant by 'a thought arising in the office of debt.
14. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it for a single mind to give rise to a thought?"
Nāgasena said: "The śramaṇa unifies his mind;
he reflects that throughout the events of a thousand billion lifetimes since his birth, it is this very self that persists, and thus he generates the thought by unifying his mind."
15. The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is meant by one who recites and generates mindfulness through study? Nāgasena replied:

“The Emperor possesses ancient books; when he reflects, thinking, ‘This was a book written by such-and-such an emperor in such-and-such a year,’ this is what is meant by ‘the arising of recollection from having read a book.
16. The King asked Nāgasena again:
“What is it that, having once been entrusted [to memory], gives rise to recollection upon being seen again?”

Nāgasena said: "If a person has something entrusted to them, and upon seeing it again with their own eyes, a thought arises; this is what is meant by 'a thought arising regarding that which was entrusted.
The King said:
"Excellent! The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Does the Buddha truly know all things of the past, the present, and the future?"
Nāgasena said: "Indeed. The Buddha knows all."
The king said:
"If the Buddha knows all matters completely, for what reason does he not instruct his disciples all at once?
For what reason does he instruct them gradually?"
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Does there not happen to be a physician in the kingdom?
The king replied:
“There is a physician.
“Is he able to know all the medicines in the world?
The king said:
"He is able to identify all medicinal herbs.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"When a physician treats an illness, does he administer the medicine all at once, or does he give it to him gradually?"
The king said, "One must not administer medicine preemptively to a person who is not yet ill; one administers medicine only when there is an illness. Nāgasena said:

"Although the Buddha fully knows all matters of the past, future, and present, he cannot instruct all the people of the world simultaneously; rather, he must gradually bestow upon them the sutras and precepts so that they may practice and uphold them."
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:

"You śramaṇas say: 'If a person commits evil while in the world, yet at the point of death after reaching a hundred years of age, they recollect the Buddha, then all such deceased persons shall be reborn in the heavens.'"
"I do not believe these words.
He spoke again:
"If one kills a single living being, upon death one shall immediately enter hell."
"I do not believe these words.
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person were to take a small stone and place it upon the water; would the stone float or sink?"
The king said, "The stone has sunk. Nāgasena replied:
“If one were to place a hundred large stones upon a boat, would that boat sink?
The King said, “It would not sink.”
Nāgasena said: "A hundred large stones within a boat do not sink because of the boat.
Although a person may possess inherent evil, if they for a moment bring to mind the Buddha, by virtue of this, they do not enter the hells and instead attain birth in the heavens."
"As for those small stones that sank, they are like people who commit evil and do not know the Buddhist scriptures; after death, they immediately enter the *niraya* hells.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"For what purpose do you practice the Way and become śramaṇas?
Nāgasena replied:
"Desiring to abandon all suffering—past suffering, present suffering, and future suffering—and not wishing to undergo it again, I practice the path of training as a śramaṇa."
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If suffering occurs only in future lives, why do people study the Path and become śramaṇas beforehand?
Nāgasena asked the King:
"Does Your Majesty perhaps have an enemy state or a rival who wishes to attack you?
The King replied, "Indeed."
"There is an enemy state and a hostile kinsman who constantly desire to attack one another.
Nāgasena asked the king,
"When the enemy lord was about to arrive, did Your Majesty then prepare weapons of war, equip your defenses, and dig moats?"
"Should one prepare for this in advance?
The King replied,
"One ought to have provisions and preparations ready beforehand."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"For what reason do you prepare provisions in advance?
The king replied:
"Because one must be prepared for the enemy's arrival at any time.
Nāgasena asked the king, "The enemy has not yet arrived; why do you prepare for him in advance?"
Nāgasena asked the king again:
"Is it only when one is hungry that one sows in the fields, or only when one is thirsty that one digs a well?
The king replied:
"One should prepare everything in advance. Nāgasena said:
"Since you are not yet hungry or thirsty, why do you make preparations in advance?"
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"How far is it from here to the seventh Brahma Heaven?
Nāgasena replied, "It is very far."
"Let a rock as large as the king’s palace fall from the seventh Brahma heaven; it will take six months for it to reach this earth.
The King said, "You śramaṇas say: "
Having attained the path of Arhatship, he flew up to the seventh Brahma Heaven in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm.
The King said, "I do not believe this."
"To travel several tens of thousands of *li*, how can it be so swift?
Nāgasena asked the king,
"In what country was Your Majesty originally born?"
The king said, "I was originally born in the Great Qin country; its name is Ali-xian.
Nāgasena asked the king:
"How many *li* is it from here to Aḷakamandā?
The King replied,
"It is two thousand *yojanas*, which amounts to eighty thousand *li*."
Nāgasena asked the king, "Have you ever,
while here, thought of matters concerning your own kingdom from afar?
The king replied:
"It is so; I am merely constantly thinking of the affairs of my own country. Nāgasena said:
"Your Majesty, please try once more to recall matters from your native land— anything you ever did there?
The King said,
"I have already recalled them."
Nāgasena said: "When Your Majesty travels eighty thousand li, how is it that you return so quickly?
The King replied:
"Excellent! The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If two people were to die here at the same time—one reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven and the other born in Kaśmīra, seven hundred and twenty li from here—who would arrive first?"
Nāgasena said, "Both arrived at the same time. The king said:
"The distance between them is very great; how is it that you both arrived together?
Nāgasena asked the king, "Try now to think of the country of Aḷaka."
The king said, "I have already considered it.
Nāgasena spoke again:
"Your Majesty, please try again and think of Kaśmīra. The King said,
"I have already thought of it."
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Between these two countries, which one suffers more?
The king replied:
"They are exactly the same," Nāgasena said.
"If two people die together, and one is reborn in the seventh Brahmā Heaven while the other is reborn in Kaśmīra, they are nonetheless equal."
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose there were a pair of birds flying together; one bird perched upon a great tree, and the other bird perched upon a small, low tree."
"When both birds have come to rest together, whose shadow will reach the ground first?
The king replied,
"Their shadows will reach the ground simultaneously."
Nāgasena said: "Both men die together;
one is born in the seventh Brahma-heaven and the other is born in Kaśmīra, yet they both arrive at the same time."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
“How many things does a person employ to learn the Way?
Nāgasena replied,
“One employs seven things to learn the Way.”

What are the seven? First, mindfulness of good and evil matters; second, diligence; third, delighting in the Path; fourth, subduing the mind to do good; fifth, mindfulness of the Path; sixth, single-mindedness; seventh, meeting circumstances with neither aversion nor attachment.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"Does a person learn the Way by means of these seven things?
Nāgasena replied:
"One does not fully know the Path through learning by means of all seven matters.
The wise person, possessing wisdom, discerns good and evil; it is by means of this one matter that they discern them.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"If one can know by means of a single matter, why do you speak of seven matters?
Nāgasena asked the king, "Suppose a person holds a sword in its scabbard and leans it against a wall; would that sword be able to cut anything of its own accord?"
The king said, "I am unable to cut anything. Nāgasena said:
"Although the human mind is luminous, it must necessarily rely on these six matters together to constitute wisdom.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"When a person performs good deeds, is the merit obtained great?
When they perform evil deeds, is the calamity incurred great?"
Nāgasena said: "When a person performs good deeds, they receive great merit; when they perform evil deeds, they receive small retribution.
If a person commits an evil deed but daily repents their transgression, for that reason their transgression becomes smaller each day."
"When others perform good deeds, they think of them with joy day and night; for this reason, they obtain great merit. Nāgasena said:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a man in that country who was stump-like, lacking hands and feet, yet he took a lotus flower and offered it to the Buddha."
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This child with hands and feet like a tree stump shall, after ninety-one kalpas, no longer fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, but shall attain birth in the heavens."
"When their life in heaven comes to an end, they return once more to become human beings.
For this reason, I know that when a person performs even a small good deed, the merit obtained is great.

As for those who commit evil, the person themselves feels remorse; as the days pass, the transgression is diminished and exhausted. For this reason, I know that when a person commits a transgression, the resulting calamity is small.
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Between a wise person who commits evil and a foolish person who commits evil, which of these two incurs the greater retribution?
Nāgasena replied,
"The foolish person who commits evil incurs great retribution, while the wise person who commits evil incurs little retribution."
The king said: "It is not as Nāgasena has said.
The king spoke thus.
"The laws of our state punish high ministers severely for their transgressions, yet punish the ignorant common people lightly.
Therefore, when the wise commit evil, they incur great calamity; when the foolish commit evil, they incur little calamity."
Nāgasena asked the king:

"Suppose there were a piece of heated iron on the ground; one person knew it was heated iron while another did not. If both went forward to take hold of the heated iron, whose hands would suffer more from the burn?"
The King said,
"If one does not know, the punishment for cutting off the hand is great. Nāgasena said:
"The fool commits evil and cannot repent of it himself; therefore, his calamity is great.
The wise person commits evil but knows it is improper to have done so; he repents his transgressions daily, and therefore his calamity is small."
The king said, "Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Is there anyone who can take this body and fly upward as far as the seventh Brahma-heaven, or reach the land of Uttarakuru, or go to whatever place they desire?"
Nāgasena said, "I can. The king said:
"How can one carry this body to the seventh Brahma heaven, or to the land of Uttarakuru, or to wherever one wishes to go?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Do you not recall, O King, when as a young child you leaped across a space of ten feet while playing?"
The king said, "When I was young,
I had the thought to leap, and I could leap over a space of more than ten feet. Nāgasena said:
"One who has attained the Way can, if they so desire, leap as far as the seventh Brahma Heaven; it is the same when reaching the land of Uttarakuru.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Your various śramaṇas say that there are bones four thousand li in length."
"What kind of body and bones could be as long as four thousand *li*?
Nāgasena asked the king,
"Have you not heard that in the great ocean there is a large fish named Tsai (Timitimiṅgila), whose body is twenty-eight thousand *li* in length?"
The king said, “Indeed. It is so; we have heard of this.”
Nāgasena said, “If there is a fish twenty-eight thousand *li* long, its rib-bone would be four thousand *li* in length; why does Your Majesty find this strange?
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"You monks, you say: 'We are able to sever the matter of breathing.
The king said:
"How can one cut off the breath?
Nāgasena asked the king.
"Have you ever heard of 'volition' (cetanā)?"
The King said, "I have heard it. Nāgasena said:
“Do you think, O King, that the aspiration lies within the human body?
The King replied,
“I believe the aspiration lies within the human body.”
Nāgasena said: "Your Majesty, one who is considered a fool—unable to restrain his body and speech and unable to uphold the sūtras and precepts—even such a person does not delight in his own body."

Nāgasena said: "As for those who practice the Way, if they can restrain body and speech, uphold the sūtras and precepts, and unify their minds, they will attain the four dhyānas and thereby become able to cease breathing altogether."
The king said, "Excellent! Then the king asked Nāgasena:
"If one calls it 'ocean,' is this water named 'ocean' because of that,
or is it called 'ocean' for some other reason? Nāgasena replied:
"The reason people call it the 'sea' is that water and salt are present in equal proportions; for this reason, it is called the sea.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"For what reason is the sea entirely salty, with a taste like salt?"

Nāgasena said: "The reason the seawater is salty is that it has been brackish for a vast duration; furthermore, many fish, turtles, and insects discharge their waste into the water, and for this reason it has become salty."
The king said, “Excellent! The king then asked Nāgasena again:
"Once a person has attained the Way, can they contemplate all profound matters? Nāgasena replied, "Yes."
"When a person attains the Way, they are able to contemplate all profound matters.
Nāgasena said: "The Buddhist scriptures are most profound; they encompass knowledge of all things."
"Immeasurable matters shall all be adjudicated with impartial wisdom by you.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king asked Nāgasena again:
"Regarding these three things—the person (pudgala), the spirit (ātman), and nature (prakṛti)—are they identical or are they distinct?
Nāgasena replied:
“The human spirit is that which gives rise to awareness; the wise person understands the Way; that which is spontaneous is empty space, wherein no person exists.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
“What is meant by ‘attaining a person,’ and who is it that attains a person?”

The eye perceives forms, the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the mouth knows tastes, the body perceives textures such as coarse or soft, and the mind knows matters of good and evil; what is it that constitutes a "person"?
Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose a man were able to see with his own eyes, but someone were to remove his pupils; would his vision not then be more vast and far-reaching?
Or suppose one were to tear open and enlarge his ears; would his hearing of sounds not then be more vast and far-reaching?"
If one were to enlarge the nostrils, would one’s perception of fragrances thereby increase?
If one were to widen the mouth, would one’s discernment of flavors thereby increase?
If one were to flay the skin and flesh, would one thereby gain a more certain knowledge of what is coarse or soft?
"If one were to uproot that intention, would the resulting thoughts not be even more numerous?
The King replied, "No."
Nāgasena said: "The deeds performed by the Buddha were exceedingly difficult; the likeness of the Buddha is most wondrous.
The King asked Nāgasena again:
"What is it that you have accomplished so difficult, and what is it so marvelous? Nāgasena replied,
"The Buddha said that he can know the contents within a person's belly and can fully understand everything seen by the eye."

One is able to resolve matters concerning the eye, resolve matters concerning the ear, resolve matters concerning the nose, resolve matters concerning the mouth, resolve matters concerning the body, resolve matters concerning failure, resolve matters concerning doubt, resolve matters concerning what is thought, and resolve matters concerning the spirit.
Nāgasena said: "If a person were to take up seawater in his mouth, would he be able to distinguish whether the water in his mouth was from a spring, a certain flowing stream, or a certain river?"
The King said,
"When all the waters have merged into one, it is difficult to know them individually. Nāgasena said:
“The Buddha’s deeds are difficult to perform; he is able to distinguish and know the flavors of all these waters.
Now, regarding the seawater seen before one's eyes, even the King cannot distinguish its flavor. Yet, that which is not seen by humans or gods—the six things within the human body—is invisible.”
Nāgasena said: "Therefore, the Buddha understands them;

from the mental intention to what is seen by the eyes, from the mental intention to what is heard by the ears, from the mental intention to what is smelled by the nose, from the mental intention to the taste known by the mouth, from the mental intention to the sensations of pain, pleasure, cold, heat, roughness, and hardness known by the body, and from the mental intention toward whatever object it is directed—the Buddha knows, discerns, and understands them all."
The king said, "Excellent! Nāgasena said:
"It is already midnight; I wish to depart.
The King immediately commanded his attendants:
"Take four pieces of fine cotton cloth, soak them in sesame oil, and hold them as torches to escort Nāgasena back."
"Serve Nāgasena as you would serve my own person.
The attendants all replied,
"We shall obey your instructions."
The King said, "If one can obtain a teacher such as Nāgasena and have a disciple such as myself, the Way may be attained swiftly.

Whatever questions the King asked, Nāgasena answered each matter immediately; the King was greatly delighted and immediately took from his inner treasury fine garments worth more than one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and presented them to Nāgasena.
The King said to Nāgasena:
"From this day forward, I wish for you, Nāgasena, to dine together with eight hundred monks within my palace; furthermore, whatever you require shall be obtained from me, the King."
Nāgasena replied to the king:
"I am a man of the Way; I have almost no desires.
The king said:
"Nagasena, you should protect yourself, and you should also protect my person. Nagasena said:
"In what way should I protect myself and protect the King's person?"
The king replied,
"I fear people will debate and call me stingy;
although Nāgasena has resolved all my doubts for me, I am unable to grant him anything."
The King said, "I fear some might say:
'Nāgasena was unable to resolve the King's doubts; therefore, the King did not grant him a reward.
The King spoke thus.
“Nāgasena, may I obtain his merit, and Nāgasena shall likewise protect his reputation.
The King said:
“It is like a lion within a golden cage; though confined, it always has the desire to depart.”
"Although I am now a king and reside within the palace precincts, my heart finds no joy; I wish to renounce the kingdom and depart to practice the Way.
When the King had finished speaking, Nāgasena rose and returned to the Buddhist monastery.
Just as Nāgasena had departed, the king thought to himself:
"For what matters did I question Nāgasena?
What matters has Nāgasena explained for me?"
The king thought to himself:
"I hope that Nāgasena has not failed to understand my meaning.
Nāgasena, upon returning to the monastery, also thought to himself:
"What matter will the King ask me?
And what matter shall I answer the King?
Nāgasena thought to himself:
"Whatever Your Majesty asks, I shall explain it all for you.

Thinking of this until dawn, the next day Nāgasena donned his *kāṣāya* robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered the palace directly to take his seat upon the dais. After the King had paid homage to Nāgasena, he withdrew to sit down.
The king said to Nāgasena:
"Just as Nāgasena had departed, I thought to myself:
'What question should I ask Nāgasena?'"
"What words will Nāgasena reply to me?
I further thought to myself:
"May Nāgasena not fail to understand my meaning regarding what I have asked."
"I recalled these words and, filled with joy, lay down in peace until dawn. Nāgasena said:
"As I was returning home, I too thought to myself:"
"What matter will the King ask me about?
What matter shall I explain to the King?
I further reflected to myself:
"Whatever Your Majesty asks, I shall immediately explain it for you.
Because of this, he remained joyful until dawn.
When he had finished speaking, Nāgasena wished to depart, and the king rose and paid him homage.
The Sutra of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena, Volume II
